R.q:
The so-called wellness program at Harmon Industries is a disaster. Fewer than 22 percent of employees signed up last year, and the company paid a consulting firm $180,000 to run it. Workers were bombarded with nagging emails about step counts, and the heavily promoted health screenings drew only 140 people out of 2,300. Anyone who thinks this program is helping employees has not been paying attention.

Which of the following best describes the passage?
o: It is objective, because it is written in the third person.
It is subjective, because it is written from the employees' view.
It is objective, because its claims are based on numbers.
It is subjective, because its word choice shows a clear slant.
R.w: The statistics are factual, but "so-called," "disaster," "bombarded" and "nagging" reveal the author's negative judgment. Slanted word choice makes a text subjective even when it includes numbers.

n.0: Third-person writing can be subjective; this passage uses third person yet clearly argues a judgment.
n.1: The passage is subjective, but not because of whose view it reflects; the author never says employees share this view. The slanted wording is what makes it subjective.
n.2: Statistics do not make a text neutral. The author selects and frames the numbers with loaded language to support a strong opinion.

R.q:
Leah's grandfather was just told he has type 2 diabetes, and she wants reliable information about meal planning to share with him. Her search turns up four websites, listed with what she can tell about each.
Site 1: a .gov page from a national health agency, reviewed by physicians, updated this year
Site 2: a .org page from a group that sells a meal-replacement shake, updated this year
Site 3: a personal blog by a man who manages his diabetes with diet, updated last month
Site 4: a .edu page written by a nutrition student for a class project in 2009

Which site is most likely to be credible?
o: Site 3, because it reflects personal experience with the condition
Site 1, because it is current, reviewed, and from a health authority
Site 4, because .edu sites are written by universities and are reliable
Site 2, because nonprofit .org sites do not sell products to readers
R.w: Site 1 meets the credibility checks: authority (a national health agency), accuracy (physician review), and currency (updated this year).

n.0: One person's experience is anecdotal and not reviewed by experts.
n.2: This page is a student project from 2009, so it lacks expert authority and is out of date.
n.3: A .org address does not guarantee neutrality; this group sells a product, which is a conflict of interest.

R.q:
From a supplement company's website: MemoryMax sharpens your memory in just two weeks! In a study by a university lab, 12 adults took MemoryMax every morning for 14 days. At the end of the study, they recalled more words from a list than they had on the first day. No other group was tested. Order now and see the difference for yourself.

Which statement best evaluates the study described on the website?
o: It is unreliable because it was carried out by a university lab instead of the company.
It is sufficient to prove the claim because it measured memory directly over time.
It is relevant to the claim but too limited to establish that the product works.
It is irrelevant to the claim because it measured word recall rather than memory.
R.w: The study does test memory, so it is relevant. But 12 people, two weeks, and no comparison group cannot rule out practice effects (people get better at the same task with repetition), so it is not sufficient.

n.0: Independent testing usually adds credibility; the weakness is the study's size and design.
n.1: With no comparison group, the improvement could come from practice; measuring memory does not make the study sufficient.
n.3: Recalling words from a list is a memory measure, so the study is relevant.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Many people believe that food dropped on the floor is safe to eat if it is picked up within five seconds. Researchers who tested this idea dropped several foods, including watermelon, bread and gummy candy, onto surfaces coated with harmless bacteria. Bacteria reached some foods in less than one second. Time on the floor did matter, since longer contact transferred more bacteria, but the type of food mattered more. Wet watermelon picked up the most bacteria, while gummy candy picked up the least. The surface mattered too: carpet passed fewer bacteria to food than tile or stainless steel did. Speed, it turns out, is a poor guide to whether dropped food is clean.

Which title best fits the passage?
o: Testing the Five-Second Rule
How Bacteria Spread Through the Home
The Five-Second Rule Holds Up in the Lab
Watermelon: The Riskiest Food to Drop
R.w: A good title names the topic and fits the whole passage. The passage describes an experiment that tested the five-second belief and concludes that speed is a poor guide, so "Testing the Five-Second Rule" covers the entire text.

n.1: Too broad: the passage covers transfer from a floor surface to dropped food, not bacteria throughout a home.
n.2: Opposite of the passage: bacteria transferred in under one second, so the rule did not hold up.
n.3: Too narrow: watermelon is one result within the experiment, not the subject of the whole passage.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Every evening at six, Mr. Okafor carried a folding chair to the end of his driveway and sat facing the street until the streetlights came on. Neighbors waved, and he waved back but rarely spoke. On the day a moving truck arrived at the house across the street, he stayed out past dark. The next evening, a young woman from the new family crossed the street with a plate of cookies. Mr. Okafor stood, unfolded a second chair that had been leaning behind his own, and offered it to her.

Which inference about Mr. Okafor is best supported by the passage?
o: He sits outside each evening in order to watch for moving trucks.
He dislikes his longtime neighbors and prefers to be left alone.
He was open to company, though he rarely started conversations himself.
He has been lonely since his wife passed away a short time ago.
R.w: He rarely speaks first, yet he had a second chair ready and offered it as soon as someone approached. Those details support the idea that he welcomed company even though he did not seek it out.

n.0: Distortion: he sits out every evening; the moving truck appeared on one day only.
n.1: Contradicted: he waves back at neighbors and offers the visitor a chair.
n.3: An assumption: the passage never mentions a wife or any loss.

R.q:
Isabel plans to apply to registered nursing programs in her state for next fall. She needs a complete list of the state's approved programs and each program's current admission requirements, including the minimum TEAS score it expects. Her school counselor has warned her that requirements often change from one year to the next. She has bookmarked several sources to check before the first application deadline.

Which choice would best give Isabel the information she needs?
o: An encyclopedia article explaining the different types of nursing degrees
An online forum where applicants post the TEAS scores that got them admitted
The state board's list of approved programs and each school's admissions page
A national magazine ranking and a college guidebook, both from three years ago
R.w: Step 1: the state board of nursing is the authority that approves programs, so its list is complete and official. Step 2: each school's own admissions page gives its current requirements for next fall.

n.0: An encyclopedia explains degree types in general; it does not list programs or their requirements.
n.1: Applicants' reported scores are anecdotal and are not the schools' official requirements.
n.3: Both are three years old and requirements change yearly; neither is the official list of approved programs or a school's current requirements.

R.q:
Passage 1
A young beaver tried to build a dam alone. Each night the current carried away his branches, and each morning he began again, too proud to call the older beavers downstream. At last, worn out, he asked. By sunset, five of them had built what he had failed to build in a week.

Passage 2
In her first month as a new graduate nurse, Kim stayed late every night to finish her charting. She was sure that asking her preceptor for shortcuts would look weak. When she finally asked, her preceptor showed her how to chart at the bedside, and Kim began leaving on time. "I wish I had asked in week one," she said.

Which theme is developed in both passages?
o: Pride can keep people from help that would make their work easier.
Experienced workers should seek out newcomers who need training.
Working longer hours is the surest way to master a new task.
Animals and people learn new skills in very different ways.
R.w: The beaver is too proud to ask the older beavers, and Kim fears that asking will look weak. In both, asking finally solves the problem, so both develop the idea that pride blocks useful help.

n.1: Neither text says experienced workers should seek out newcomers; in both, the newcomer finally asks.
n.2: Both texts show long hours failing; success comes from asking for help.
n.3: The passages show the beaver and Kim learning the same lesson, so they are parallel, not contrasted.

R.q:
Passage 1
At mile 22 of her first marathon, Gloria's left calf cramped so badly that she sat down on the curb. Volunteers offered her a ride to the finish. She shook her head, stood, and walked, then jogged, one streetlight at a time. She crossed the line after the clocks had been switched off.

Passage 2
When the river flooded the Ashton library, it ruined 30,000 books. For eight months, volunteers sorted donations on folding tables in the high school gym, a few boxes each evening. Last week, the library reopened with full shelves and a new reading room.

Which theme do both passages share?
o: Finishing a hard race matters more than the time on the clock.
Steady effort, step by step, can carry people through great difficulty.
Floods and other disasters test the resources of small towns.
Communities grow stronger when neighbors give their time to one another.
R.w: Gloria finishes by going one streetlight at a time, and the library is rebuilt a few boxes each evening over eight months. Both show persistence in small steps overcoming a setback.

n.0: This fits Passage 1 only; Passage 2 is not about a race.
n.2: This names a topic of Passage 2 and does not apply to Passage 1.
n.3: Community volunteering fits Passage 2, but Gloria turns down help and finishes on her own.

R.q:
Read the table of contents of an anatomy textbook.

Contents
Preface, page vii
Chapter 1: Cells and Tissues, page 1
Chapter 2: The Skeletal System, page 27
Chapter 3: The Muscular System, page 58
Chapter 4: The Nervous System, page 84
Chapter 5: The Endocrine System, page 121
Chapter 6: The Cardiovascular System, page 147
Chapter 7: The Digestive System, page 176
Appendix: Laboratory Values, page 389
Glossary, page 402
Index, page 415

A student wants to find every page in the book that mentions the hormone insulin. Which part of the book should she use?
o: The index, beginning on page 415
The glossary, beginning on page 402
Chapter 5, beginning on page 121
The appendix, beginning on page 389
R.w: An index lists specific topics alphabetically with every page on which each one appears, so it is the tool for finding all mentions of insulin across chapters.

n.1: A glossary defines key terms; it does not list the pages where a term appears.
n.2: The endocrine chapter likely discusses insulin, but a chapter listing gives only where the chapter starts, not every page in the book that mentions insulin.
n.3: The appendix holds supplementary laboratory values, not a list of page references.

R.q:
Passage 1
From a high school teacher: This year our school began collecting phones at the front office each morning. Students pick them up at dismissal. Parents who need to reach their child during the day call the office, and we deliver the message within minutes. Since the change, I see students talking to each other at lunch, and fewer students drift off in class.

Passage 2
From a student: Taking our phones all day puts us at risk. If there is an emergency, or if my mom needs to tell me that my ride has changed, how is she supposed to reach me?

Based on Passage 1, how would its author most likely respond to the concern in Passage 2?
o: Families can still reach students through the school office.
Students should keep their phones on silent inside their bags.
Emergencies at school are too rare to plan for in a policy.
Students who need their phones may use them during lunch.
R.w: The teacher explains that parents call the office and messages are delivered within minutes. That arrangement directly answers the student's worry about being reached.

n.1: The teacher supports collecting phones at the office, so keeping them in bags conflicts with Passage 1.
n.2: The teacher never dismisses emergencies; Passage 1 describes a way to handle urgent messages.
n.3: Passage 1 says phones stay at the office until dismissal, so lunch use is not part of the policy.

R.q:
Read the directions.

Returning Your Sample Kit
Seal the sample tube inside the clear biohazard bag, but first wrap the tube in the absorbent pad. Place the sealed bag in the white box. After the bag is in the box, slip the completed request form into the box's outer pocket; do not put the form inside the bag. Once the form is in the pocket, tape the box shut, and drop it off at any post office within 24 hours of collecting the sample.

Place the steps in the order the directions require, starting with the first.
o: Slip the request form into the outer pocket
Place the sealed bag in the white box
Drop the box off at a post office
Seal the tube inside the biohazard bag
Wrap the tube in the absorbent pad
Tape the box shut
R.w: The first sentence is written out of order: "but first" means the tube is wrapped in the pad before it is sealed in the bag. The sealed bag then goes in the box, the form goes in the outer pocket after the bag is in the box, the box is taped once the form is in place, and it is dropped off.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Visiting Hours at Maple Grove Rehabilitation Center
General visitors are welcome from 11 a.m. to 8 p.m. on weekdays and from 9 a.m. to 8 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays. Because therapy sessions run each weekday morning, the center asks that weekday visits not begin before 11. Children under 12 may visit at any time during visiting hours if an adult accompanies them. Each resident may have up to three visitors at once in a room; larger groups may use the second-floor sunroom from noon to 6 p.m. daily. Overnight stays by family members are allowed in the private suites on the third floor and must be arranged with the nurse manager in advance.

According to the passage, what is the earliest time a general visitor may arrive on a Sunday?
o: 9 a.m.
Noon
6 p.m.
R.w: Weekend hours (Saturdays and Sundays) begin at 9 a.m.

n.0: 11 a.m. is the weekday start time, set because of weekday morning therapy.
n.2: Noon is when the sunroom opens for larger groups, not when visiting hours begin.
n.3: 6 p.m. is when the sunroom closes to groups.

R.q:
Starting March 1, the county health department will require all restaurant employees who handle food to complete a two-hour safety course. The course is offered online and in person, costs $15 and covers handwashing, safe cooking temperatures and food storage.

Restaurant owners, do not wait. Classes are already filling up, and any employee without a certificate after March 1 will be barred from the kitchen. Sign your staff up today.

Which of the following best describes how the tone changes from the first paragraph to the second?
o: It moves from humorous to serious.
It moves from optimistic to pessimistic.
It moves from critical to celebratory.
It moves from objective to urgent.
R.w: The first paragraph reports the rule's details neutrally. The second uses commands ("do not wait," "sign your staff up today") and a warning about filling classes, which creates urgency.

n.0: The first paragraph contains no humor; it lists dates, costs and topics.
n.1: Neither paragraph expresses hope or gloom about the outcome; the second paragraph pushes for quick action rather than predicting a bad result.
n.2: Neither paragraph criticizes the rule or celebrates it; the shift is from reporting to pressing for action.

R.q:
Letter to the student newspaper: The faculty senate is considering a policy that would let students retake one failed exam per course. This would be a mistake. If students know they can retake an exam, they will stop studying for first attempts. Soon nearly every exam will be taken twice, instructors will spend their time writing makeup tests instead of teaching, and within a few years employers will stop taking our degrees seriously.

Which fallacy does the letter contain?
o: Circular reasoning
Post hoc
Hasty generalization
Slippery slope
R.w: The writer claims one small policy will set off a chain of worsening results (no studying, every exam taken twice, worthless degrees) without evidence for each step. That is a slippery slope.

n.0: Circular reasoning restates its conclusion as its reason; the letter gives a (weak) chain of causes.
n.1: Post hoc claims a past event caused a later one because it came first; the letter predicts future consequences instead.
n.2: A hasty generalization draws a broad conclusion from a few examples; the letter offers no examples.

R.q:
Survey of 400 volunteers at Grandview Hospital: "How did you first hear about our volunteer program?"
Friend or family member | 45%
Hospital website | 25%
Social media | 20%
Newspaper ad | 10%

At a planning meeting, the volunteer coordinator said she wants to spend most of next year's outreach budget on newspaper ads. "The newspaper brought in 40 volunteers," she said, "which is more than we expected."

Which statement best combines the survey results with the coordinator's statement?
o: Her figure of 40 conflicts with the survey, which shows only 10.
Her 40 volunteers are accurate but are the smallest group in the survey.
The newspaper brought in more volunteers than social media did.
Most volunteers first heard about the program through online sources.
R.w: Ten percent of 400 is 40, so her figure matches the survey. But the newspaper is the smallest source; friends and family (180), the website (100), and social media (80) each brought in more volunteers.

n.0: This treats 10 percent as a count; 10 percent of 400 volunteers is 40, matching her figure.
n.2: Social media accounts for 20 percent, or 80 volunteers, twice the newspaper's 40.
n.3: The website and social media together make up 45 percent, which is less than half.

R.q:
Oral and tympanic thermometers are both common in clinics. An oral thermometer is placed under the tongue and takes about 10 to 40 seconds to give a reading, depending on the model. A tympanic thermometer, by contrast, reads the temperature inside the ear in one to two seconds. Both give reliable results when used correctly. However, oral readings can be thrown off if a patient has just had a hot or cold drink, whereas tympanic readings can be affected by earwax or a poorly placed probe.

Which organizational structure does the author use?
o: chronological order
description
classification into types
compare and contrast
R.w: The passage sets two thermometers side by side, noting similarities ("both") and differences ("by contrast," "however," "whereas"). That is compare-and-contrast structure.

n.0: Times appear (seconds per reading), but the passage does not narrate events or steps in order.
n.1: Each thermometer is described, but the descriptions are arranged to show how the two are alike and different, which makes the structure comparative.
n.2: Classification sorts many items into categories; this passage weighs two specific devices against each other.

R.q:
Read the passage.

After Brookside Hospital placed hand-sanitizer dispensers outside every patient room on its surgical unit, managers tracked how often staff cleaned their hands. Before the change, observers saw staff clean their hands at about half of the moments when they should have. Six months later, the rate had risen to about three quarters. Over the same period, the number of infections patients picked up on the unit fell by about a fifth. During those six months, the hospital also hired two infection-prevention nurses, who ran training sessions on every unit.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
o: Hand cleaning rose after the change, though the dispensers may not be the sole reason for it.
The dispensers probably did more than the nurses' training to raise hand cleaning.
Infections on the unit fell by about three quarters, likely because hand cleaning improved.
The infection-prevention nurses, rather than the dispensers, caused the drop in infections.
R.w: The rate of hand cleaning clearly rose (from about half to about three quarters), but the new nurses' training happened during the same six months. The evidence supports the rise while leaving the cause uncertain, which is what this option says.

n.1: Unsupported: the dispensers and the training began in the same six months, and the passage gives no way to compare their effects.
n.2: Misreads the figures: infections fell by about a fifth; about three quarters is the new hand-cleaning rate.
n.3: Unsupported: the passage gives no way to separate the effect of the training from the effect of the dispensers.

R.q:
Our school district's plan to give every high school student a free tablet has real promise. Students without computers at home would finally be able to complete online assignments, and teachers could share lessons more easily. Still, I have questions. The district has not explained who will repair broken devices, and it has budgeted no money for training teachers to use them well. If those gaps are filled before the fall, I will be among the plan's strongest supporters.

Which of the following best describes the author's attitude toward the tablet plan?
o: opposed, with a few exceptions
supportive, with reservations
enthusiastic, with no concerns
neutral, with no stated view
R.w: The author praises the plan's "real promise" but raises questions about repairs and training, and promises full support only if those gaps are filled. Support with conditions is a qualified, or cautiously supportive, attitude.

n.0: The author's main stance is favorable; the concerns are conditions for full support, not reasons to oppose the plan.
n.2: The author raises two specific concerns, so the support is not unqualified.
n.3: The author clearly expresses a view ("real promise," "I have questions"), so the passage is not neutral.

R.q:
Read the passage.

The Westbrook Public Health Department offered free flu shots at three locations last October. The downtown clinic, open weekdays from 9 a.m. to 4 p.m., gave 410 shots. A kiosk at the mall, open weekday evenings and all day on weekends, gave 1,280. A mobile van that parked outside large workplaces at lunchtime gave 960. This year the department has the same budget and staff, and it plans to close one of the three locations.

Which conclusion is best supported by the passage?
o: Many residents found it easier to get a shot outside standard weekday business hours.
Residents who live downtown were less worried about the flu than residents elsewhere.
Most residents would rather get a flu shot at work than at a clinic or a mall.
The department will close the mall kiosk because it costs the most to operate.
R.w: The location open evenings and weekends gave the most shots (1,280), more than three times the weekday-hours clinic (410). That pattern best supports the conclusion that many people found off-hours more convenient.

n.1: Unsupported: the downtown clinic's location and hours explain the lower number as well as any attitude; the passage says nothing about worry.
n.2: Overreaches: the workplace van gave fewer shots (960) than the mall kiosk, so "most residents" prefer work is not supported.
n.3: Unsupported: the passage gives no costs and does not say which location will close.

R.q:
Tanya's four-year-old son, who weighs 36 pounds, has a fever. The pediatrician's nurse told her by phone that she may give him children's acetaminophen, but the office is now closed for the night. Tanya has a new, unopened bottle of the medicine at home and wants to be sure she gives the correct amount for his weight. She considers four sources of information.

Which source should Tanya rely on for the dose?
o: A pediatric medicine handbook from 2009 on her home bookshelf
The dosing chart printed on the label of the new bottle of medicine
A parenting forum where other parents post the doses they give
A magazine article about caring for young children with fevers
R.w: The label on the product she will actually use is specific to that medicine's strength, current, and approved for use, so it is the authoritative source for the dose.

n.0: A 2009 handbook may not match the strength of today's product; for doses, currency matters.
n.2: Forum posts are anecdotal and may involve different products, strengths, or weights.
n.3: A general magazine article is not specific to this product and is not an authoritative dosing source.

R.q:
Ever since the new neighbor moved in, Mrs. Abbott has watched him from behind her curtains. "He's a scrawny young man," she told her sister, "and nosy, too. He asked me how long I'd lived here." Her sister laughed. "He sounds curious and friendly to me. And didn't you say he was lean and fit, out jogging every morning?" Mrs. Abbott frowned. "He rides that bicycle like a reckless child." Her sister shrugged. "Or like an adventurous one."

Which words from the passage carry a negative connotation? Select all that apply.
o: adventurous
curious
lean
reckless
scrawny
nosy
R.w: Mrs. Abbott chooses words with negative connotations: "scrawny" (unhealthily thin), "nosy" (intrusive) and "reckless" (dangerously careless). Her sister describes the same traits with positive words.

n.0: "Adventurous" describes the same willingness to take risks as "reckless" but suggests an appealing love of excitement, a positive connotation.
n.1: "Curious" names the same interest in others as "nosy" but with a positive connotation of healthy interest.
n.2: "Lean" describes the same thin build as "scrawny" but suggests fitness, a positive connotation.

R.q: Read the item from a community newsletter. Select the sentence that states an opinion.

parts.t: The Eastside Community Clinic opened its new dental wing in March.
The wing has four treatment chairs and is open on Saturdays from 8 a.m. to noon.
According to clinic records, the wing treated 312 patients in its first two months.
Clinic director Ana Ruiz said that most of those patients had not seen a dentist in more than a year.
Saturday hours are the most valuable service the clinic has added in a decade.
In May, the city council approved funding to add two more chairs next year.

sn.a: The Eastside Community Clinic opened its new dental wing in March.
sn.b: The wing has four treatment chairs and is open on Saturdays from 8 a.m. to noon.
sn.c: According to clinic records, the wing treated 312 patients in its first two months.
sn.d: Clinic director Ana Ruiz said that most of those patients had not seen a dentist in more than a year.
sn.e: Saturday hours are the most valuable service the clinic has added in a decade.
sn.f: In May, the city council approved funding to add two more chairs next year.

R.w: "The most valuable service" is a judgment that people could reasonably dispute, and no record or measurement could prove it. Every other sentence reports something checkable: a date, a count, opening hours, a statement someone made or a council vote.

n.a: The opening date can be confirmed in clinic records, so it is a fact.
n.b: The number of chairs and the opening hours can be verified, so this is a fact.
n.c: A count drawn from clinic records can be checked, so it is a fact.
n.d: Whether the director said this, and whether the patients' records bear it out, can both be checked. Reporting someone's words is still a factual statement.
n.f: The council's vote is a recorded event that can be confirmed now, so this is a fact even though the chairs will be added in the future.

R.q: Jordan arrives at the clinic without his appointment letter. When the kiosk displays his details, he sees that his address is out of date. Following the directions, select the one step Jordan does not complete.

parts: Self check-in at the clinic kiosk

parts.t: 1. Touch the screen to begin.
2. Scan the barcode on your appointment letter.
3. If you do not have your letter, type your date of birth instead.
4. Check that the name and address shown are correct.
5. If any detail is wrong, select "Update," correct it, and continue.
6. Take your printed ticket and wait for your number to be called.

sn.b: 2. Scan the barcode on your appointment letter.
sn.c: 3. If you do not have your letter, type your date of birth instead.
sn.d: 4. Check that the name and address shown are correct.
sn.e: 5. If any detail is wrong, select "Update," correct it, and continue.
sn.f: 6. Take your printed ticket and wait for your number to be called.

R.w: Step 2 needs the barcode on the appointment letter, and Jordan has no letter, so he skips it and uses step 3 instead. Every other step applies to him: he starts the kiosk, types his birth date, checks his details, updates the wrong address and takes a ticket.

n.a: Every user starts by touching the screen. Step 1 has no condition attached.
n.c: Step 3 is the alternative for people without a letter, which is exactly Jordan's situation, so he completes it.
n.d: Jordan must check his details. That is how he discovers that his address is out of date.
n.e: Step 5 applies when a detail is wrong. Jordan's address is wrong, so he selects Update and corrects it.
n.f: Step 5 says to correct the detail and continue, so Jordan still finishes by taking a ticket.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Before a new vaccine reaches a pharmacy shelf, it passes through several stages. The large phase 3 trial, which can include tens of thousands of volunteers, comes after a smaller phase 2 trial has helped researchers choose the right dose. Phase 2, in turn, follows phase 1, in which a few dozen healthy adults receive the vaccine so that researchers can check its safety. None of these human trials can begin until laboratory and animal studies suggest the vaccine is promising. If phase 3 shows that the vaccine is safe and effective, the company applies to the Food and Drug Administration for a license. Even after licensing, safety monitoring continues.

Place the stages in the order in which they occur, starting with the first.
o: Continued safety monitoring after licensing
Phase 2 trial to help choose the dose
Phase 1 trial in a few dozen healthy adults
Laboratory and animal studies
Phase 3 trial with thousands of volunteers
Application to the FDA for a license
R.w: The passage describes the stages backward. Laboratory and animal studies come before any human trial; phase 1 comes before phase 2, which comes before phase 3; a license is sought after phase 3; monitoring continues after licensing.

R.q:
The Harlan Medical History Museum reopened in May after an 18-month renovation. The building, which first opened in 1931, now has an elevator and wider doorways. The flu exhibit, a stunning achievement, displays nurses' letters from 1918. Admission is free on the first Sunday of each month. Visitors should plan at least two hours to see everything.

Which sentence from the passage contains both a fact and an opinion?
o: The flu exhibit, a stunning achievement, displays nurses' letters from 1918.
The building, which first opened in 1931, now has an elevator and wider doorways.
Visitors should plan at least two hours to see everything.
The museum reopened in May after an 18-month renovation.
R.w: That the exhibit displays nurses' letters from 1918 can be checked, so it is a fact. The phrase "a stunning achievement" is the writer's judgment. The sentence mixes the two.

n.1: The opening year and the building's features can be checked, so the sentence contains facts and no judgment.
n.2: "Should plan" is advice, so the sentence is an opinion, but it contains no separate checkable fact about the museum.
n.3: Both the reopening date and the length of the renovation can be confirmed, so the sentence is entirely factual.

R.q:
From a heart-health handout: Adults should aim for no more than 2,300 milligrams (mg) of sodium a day, and people with high blood pressure are often advised to stay under 1,500 mg. Most of the sodium people eat comes from packaged and restaurant foods rather than from the salt shaker.
Food (one serving) | Sodium
Canned chicken noodle soup | 890 mg
Turkey sandwich on wheat | 1,050 mg
Frozen cheese pizza (2 slices) | 1,210 mg
Garden salad with dressing | 310 mg
Mr. Alvarez has high blood pressure, and his doctor has told him to follow the lower limit.

Based on the handout and the table, which lunch by itself would put Mr. Alvarez over his daily sodium limit?
o: The soup and the salad
The pizza and the salad
The pizza by itself
The sandwich and the salad
R.w: Step 1: from the handout, his limit is 1,500 mg. Step 2: from the table, pizza plus salad is 1,210 + 310 = 1,520 mg, which is over 1,500. The other lunches total 1,200, 1,360, and 1,210 mg.

n.0: Soup and salad total 890 + 310 = 1,200 mg, under his 1,500 mg limit.
n.2: The pizza alone is 1,210 mg, under 1,500 mg.
n.3: Sandwich and salad total 1,050 + 310 = 1,360 mg, under 1,500 mg.

R.q:
Council member Ray Delgado has served the Third Ward for twelve years. Supporters call him resourceful, pointing to the new library he funded by combining three small state grants. His critics see a crafty politician who trades favors behind closed doors. Both sides agree that he is experienced and practical, and few people expect anyone to challenge him in the next election.

Which word from the passage carries a negative connotation?
o: resourceful
crafty
practical
experienced
R.w: "Crafty" means clever, but it suggests cunning or sneaky behavior. The critics use it alongside "trades favors behind closed doors," which confirms the negative connotation.

n.0: "Resourceful" also means clever at solving problems, but it carries a positive connotation; supporters use it as praise.
n.2: "Practical" is neutral to positive, suggesting sensible, realistic choices.
n.3: "Experienced" is neutral to positive; both sides use it as a fair description.

R.q:
Grayson County Hospital began in 1912 as a six-bed clinic above a hardware store. In 1925, after a fire destroyed the store, the town raised money for a two-story brick building on Elm Street. During the 1950s, the hospital added a maternity ward and its first X-ray machine. A new emergency department opened in 1978, and in 2004 the hospital joined the regional Lakeshore Health network. Today, Grayson County Hospital has 140 beds and employs more than 900 people.

Which organizational structure does the author mainly use?
o: compare and contrast
cause and effect
problem and solution
chronological order
R.w: The passage moves through the hospital's history date by date, from 1912 to today. Ordering events by time is chronological structure.

n.0: The passage traces one hospital over time; it does not set two subjects side by side.
n.1: One causal link appears (the fire led to a new building), but the passage as a whole is organized by dates, not by causes and their results.
n.2: No central problem is identified and solved; the passage lists milestones in order.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Caring for Your New Cast
For the first 48 hours, keep the injured arm raised above the level of your heart as much as possible to reduce swelling. A plaster cast takes about 48 hours to harden fully, while a fiberglass cast hardens in about 30 minutes. Keep either type dry: cover it with a plastic bag when bathing, and do not hold the cast under running water. If the cast gets damp, dry it with a hair dryer on the cool setting. Do not push objects inside the cast to scratch an itch. Call your doctor if your fingers turn blue or cold, if you cannot move them, or if the cast still feels too tight after the first 48 hours.

According to the passage, what should a patient do if the cast gets damp?
o: Cover it with a plastic bag and keep the arm raised
Wait 48 hours for the cast to harden again
Call the doctor so that the cast can be checked
Dry it with a hair dryer on the cool setting
R.w: The passage states: "If the cast gets damp, dry it with a hair dryer on the cool setting."

n.0: The plastic bag is for keeping the cast dry while bathing, and raising the arm is for swelling; neither is the step for a damp cast.
n.1: 48 hours is how long a plaster cast takes to harden at first; the passage does not say a damp cast needs to reharden.
n.2: The reasons to call the doctor are blue or cold fingers, inability to move them, or tightness after 48 hours, not dampness.

R.q:
Last year, patients at Northgate Hospital's emergency department waited an average of 74 minutes before seeing a provider, and nearly one in ten left before being seen. To address this, the hospital made three changes in January. A nurse now assesses each patient at the front door, patients with minor injuries go to a separate fast-track area, and lab tests can be ordered before a patient reaches a room. Since the changes, the average wait has dropped to 31 minutes.

Which organizational structure does the author mainly use?
o: order of importance
problem and solution
description
compare and contrast
R.w: The passage opens with a problem (long waits and patients leaving), explains the steps taken "to address this," and reports the result. That is problem-and-solution structure.

n.0: The three changes are listed as equal parts of one plan; none is ranked as most or least important.
n.2: The changes are explained as a response to a problem rather than as features described for their own sake.
n.3: The before-and-after wait times show results, but the passage is built around fixing a problem, not around comparing two subjects.

R.q:
For a nursing history assignment, Jordan chose a 1998 biography of Ada Whitfield, a nurse who opened her county's first public health clinic in 1912. The author, a historian, spent ten years studying Whitfield's clinic records, newspaper notices, and letters written by people who knew her, and the book quotes many of these documents. Jordan labeled the biography a primary source in his bibliography.

Why is Jordan's label incorrect?
o: The biography is tertiary because it covers Whitfield's entire life and career.
The biography was published long after Whitfield's death, so it cannot be primary.
The author did not live these events and interprets them from records.
The book quotes letters and notices instead of reporting the author's own views.
R.w: A biography is a secondary source because its author did not experience the events but interprets primary sources such as clinic records, newspaper notices, and letters.

n.0: Tertiary sources compile brief summaries (encyclopedias, almanacs); a researched biography is secondary.
n.1: Date alone does not decide the category; a memoir written decades later is still primary. What matters is that the author interprets others' records.
n.3: Quoting primary documents does not make a book primary, and the author does offer interpretation.

R.q:
Follow the directions.

Start with the number 4,729. Carry out the steps below in order, applying each step to the result of the step before it.
1. Swap the first digit and the last digit.
2. Add 1 to every even digit.
3. Remove the digit in the hundreds place.
4. Multiply the result by 2.
5. If the result is greater than 1,500, subtract 500 from it; otherwise, add 500 to it.

What is the final result?
R.w: Step 1: 9,724. Step 2 (2 becomes 3 and 4 becomes 5): 9,735. Step 3 removes the hundreds digit, 7: 935. Step 4: 935 x 2 = 1,870. Step 5: 1,870 is greater than 1,500, so subtract 500: 1,370.

n.1: Stops after step 4 and skips the conditional step.
n.2: Takes the wrong branch of step 5, adding 500 instead of subtracting it.
n.3: Removes the tens digit (3) instead of the hundreds digit, giving 975, then 1,950, then 1,450.

R.q:
Passage 1
One cup of water on the seedling's bed
does nothing much, the hurried gardener said.
But the girl came back with one cup every day,
and by July the vine had found its way
across the fence and up into the light,
a green thing built from mornings, small and right.

Passage 2
Researchers who study habits find that people who try to change many behaviors at once often quit within weeks. Those who start with one small action, such as a five-minute walk after breakfast, are more likely to keep going. Over months, small actions repeated daily can grow into larger routines.

Which idea do the poem and the article share?
o: Gardening is a healthy daily habit for children and teenagers.
People who change many habits at once tend to give up quickly.
Morning is the best time of day to begin a new healthy habit.
Small actions repeated over time can lead to large results.
R.w: In the poem, one cup of water a day grows a vine across the fence; in the article, small daily actions grow into larger routines. The genres differ, but the shared idea is the power of small repeated actions.

n.0: Gardening appears in the poem only, and neither text calls it a healthy habit for young people.
n.1: This finding appears in the article only; the poem says nothing about changing many habits.
n.2: The poem mentions mornings and the article's example is after breakfast, but neither claims morning is the best time.

R.q:
A post on a social media site reads: "New study proves that drinking two cups of green tea a day cuts the risk of heart disease in half! Doctors don't want you to know this." The post has been shared 50,000 times and includes a photo of a teacup but no link. Grace's aunt forwards it to her and asks whether she should start drinking green tea every day.

Which step would best help Grace judge whether the claim is accurate?
o: Count how many people have shared or liked the post.
Search for other posts that make the same green tea claim.
Find the original study that the post claims to describe.
Check how many followers the account that posted it has.
R.w: Going to the original source shows what the study actually found, how it was done, and whether "proves" and "in half" are accurate.

n.0: The number of shares measures popularity, not accuracy.
n.1: Other posts may simply copy the same claim; repetition is not independent confirmation.
n.3: A large following does not make an account reliable on health research.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Last summer, the town of Mesa Verde faced its driest season in forty years, and its reservoir fell to 30 percent of capacity. The water district asked residents to cut their use by one fifth.

The district paired the request with practical help. It offered rebates of up to $500 for replacing lawns with native plants, gave away low-flow showerheads, and posted each neighborhood's weekly water use on its website. Mayor Tina Okafor, who had replaced her own lawn with cactus and gravel, appeared in a video about the rebates.

By September, total water use had fallen 23 percent from the year before. District officials credit the neighborhood reports most of all, saying residents responded when they could compare their use with their neighbors'.

Which statements belong in a summary of the passage? Select all that apply.
o: Other towns facing a severe drought should post each neighborhood's weekly water use online.
Water use fell 23 percent, a drop officials credit mainly to the neighborhood reports.
Residents cut back mainly because $500 rebates covered the full cost of replacing a lawn.
During a severe drought, the water district asked residents to cut their use by one fifth.
Mayor Tina Okafor replaced her own lawn with cactus and gravel before appearing in a rebate video.
The district backed its request with rebates, free fixtures and neighborhood use reports.
R.w: A summary keeps each paragraph's key point in order: the drought and the request (paragraph 1), the district's support measures (paragraph 2), and the result with the officials' explanation (paragraph 3).

n.0: This is a recommendation the passage never makes; a summary adds no opinions.
n.2: Distortion: rebates were up to $500, the passage never says they covered the full cost, and officials credit the reports, not the rebates, most.
n.4: The mayor's own lawn is a minor detail; a summary leaves out such details.

R.q:
A dental hygiene student is writing a report on BrightWhite, a new whitening toothpaste. The company's website claims that the toothpaste is "safe for daily use on tooth enamel." The student wants to cite evidence on this question that her instructor will accept as trustworthy. Her instructor has told the class that a source's funding, expertise, and review process all affect how much weight its evidence deserves. She has found four possible sources.

Which source would provide the most credible evidence about the toothpaste's safety for enamel?
o: Online reviews from customers who used the toothpaste for a year
A video from a popular actress who says the product worked for her
A study designed, funded, and published by the toothpaste company
An independent lab study published in a peer-reviewed dental journal
R.w: An independent study that passed peer review has no stake in the product and was checked by other experts, so it is the most credible evidence on safety.

n.0: Customer reviews are anecdotal and cannot measure enamel damage.
n.1: An actress is not a dental expert; her endorsement is an appeal to false authority.
n.2: The company has a financial interest in a favorable result, a conflict of interest that lowers credibility.

R.q:
Parents often warn children that reading in dim light will ruin their eyesight. Eye doctors say this belief is mistaken. Reading in poor light can make the eyes feel tired and dry and may bring on a headache, but these effects go away after rest and leave no lasting damage. Nearsightedness, which has become more common among children, is linked to family history and to spending little time outdoors.

Which statement would the author identify as a misconception?
o: Reading in dim light causes lasting harm to eyesight.
Eye strain from poor lighting goes away with rest.
Reading in dim light can make the eyes feel tired.
Nearsightedness is linked to spending little time outdoors.
R.w: The passage presents the warning that dim light "will ruin" eyesight as a widely held belief that eye doctors say is mistaken, because the effects are temporary. That makes it a misconception.

n.1: The author states this directly as fact to explain why no lasting damage occurs.
n.2: The author accepts this as true; tired, dry eyes are named as a real short-term effect.
n.3: The author presents this link as accurate information about the real causes of nearsightedness.

R.q:
Read the directions and the description.

How to Use the Nasal Spray
1. Gently blow your nose.
2. Shake the bottle well and remove the cap.
3. If you are using the spray for the first time, or have not used it for 7 days or more, prime the pump by spraying it into the air until a fine mist appears.
4. Tilt your head slightly forward. Close one nostril with a finger and insert the tip into the other nostril.
5. Breathe in gently through the nose while pressing the pump once.
6. Repeat in the other nostril.
7. Wipe the tip with a clean tissue and replace the cap.

Maria last used her spray 10 days ago. This morning she blew her nose, shook the bottle and removed the cap. She tilted her head forward, closed one nostril, inserted the tip in the other, and breathed in gently while pressing the pump once. She did the same in the other nostril, then wiped the tip and replaced the cap.

Which step did Maria skip?
o: Priming the pump by spraying into the air
Tilting her head slightly forward before spraying
Wiping the tip with a clean tissue afterward
Shaking the bottle well before removing the cap
R.w: Step 3 applies when the spray has not been used for 7 days or more. Maria last used it 10 days ago, so she needed to prime the pump, and the description shows she went straight from removing the cap to spraying.

n.1: She tilted her head forward, as step 4 directs.
n.2: She wiped the tip and replaced the cap, as step 7 directs.
n.3: She shook the bottle, as step 2 directs.

R.q:
Read the passage.

Until the late 1960s, a person in the United States who needed help in an emergency had to know the local number for the police, the fire department or an ambulance service, and those numbers differed from town to town. Callers who did not know the right number often dialed the operator, who then had to find and connect the correct agency.

In 1967, a presidential commission recommended a single number for reporting emergencies nationwide. The telephone company chose 911 because it was short, easy to remember and not already used as an area code or exchange. The first 911 call was placed in Haleyville, Alabama, in February 1968.

Adoption was slow, since each community had to build its own call center, but by the end of the century most Americans could reach help by dialing the same three digits.

Which is the best summary of the passage?
o: To replace confusing local numbers, 911 became a single emergency number that spread slowly nationwide.
Before the late 1960s, callers had to know a different local emergency number or rely on an operator.
Because a 1967 commission chose 911, Haleyville, Alabama, built the nation's first emergency call center.
The phone company picked 911 because it was short, easy to remember and not used as an area code.
R.w: The passage describes the problem (many local numbers), the solution (a single number, 911, first used in 1968) and the outcome (slow adoption, then nationwide reach). This option includes all three in order.

n.1: Summarizes only the first paragraph, the problem, and leaves out the solution and its spread.
n.2: Distortion: the passage says the telephone company chose 911 and that the first call was placed in Haleyville; it never says Haleyville built the first call center.
n.3: Too narrow: the reasons for choosing 911 are a supporting detail in the second paragraph.

R.q:
Laundry detergent pods should be sold in opaque, child-resistant containers. Dr. Alicia Moreno, who has directed the county poison control center for fifteen years, says the brightly colored pods look like candy to toddlers. "In my experience, most of these calls involve children under three who found a container on a low shelf," she explains. Moreno adds that a container a toddler cannot see into or open would prevent many of the calls her staff answers each week. Manufacturers argue that warning labels are enough, but Moreno points out that toddlers cannot read.

Which type of evidence does the author mainly use to support the claim?
o: A comparison with another state's packaging laws
Testimony from an expert who works in the field
A personal story about one family's emergency
Statistics from a controlled study of poisoning cases
R.w: Nearly every supporting sentence reports what Dr. Moreno, the long-time poison control director, says from her professional experience. That is expert testimony.

n.0: No other state or law is mentioned.
n.2: No individual family's story is told; Moreno speaks in general terms about the calls her center receives.
n.3: The passage gives no study and no numbers; "most of these calls" is Moreno's experience, not statistical data.

R.q:
Read the excerpt from the index of a health textbook.

Diabetes, 112-131
   gestational, 127-128
   insipidus, 129-130
   type 1, 114-118
   type 2, 119-126
      diet and, 122-123
      exercise and, 124
Diabetic ketoacidosis, 117
Diabetic retinopathy, 125, 302
Diagnosis (see also Laboratory tests)
   of anemia, 88
   of diabetes, 116, 120
   of hypertension, 70-71
Dialysis, 204-207
Diaphragm, 140-141
Diarrhea, 188-190
Diet
   heart-healthy, 64-66
   for kidney disease, 208
   low-sodium, 72
Digestion, 176-199
   enzymes in, 181-183
   role of the liver in, 190-192
Digital thermometer, use of, 12

A student wants to read about how type 2 diabetes is diagnosed. Based on the index, which page is most likely to have this information?
o: Page 120
Page 88
Page 124
Page 116
R.w: Diagnosis of diabetes appears on pages 116 and 120. Type 2 diabetes covers pages 119-126, so page 120 is the diagnosis page that falls inside the type 2 section.

n.1: Page 88 covers the diagnosis of anemia, a different condition under the same heading.
n.2: Page 124 covers exercise and type 2 diabetes, not diagnosis.
n.3: Page 116 discusses diagnosing diabetes, but it falls in the type 1 range (114-118).

R.q:
Read the passage.

Dr. Mae Chen is best known for the community clinic she opened in Oakland in 1998, but her path there was not direct. She had first trained as a pharmacist, graduating in 1979. After six years at a hospital pharmacy, she entered medical school in 1985, the same year her daughter was born. She completed her residency in family medicine in 1992 and spent the next six years at a rural clinic in Nevada before returning to the Bay Area. Today the Oakland clinic serves more than 9,000 patients a year.

Place the events in Dr. Chen's career in the order in which they occurred, starting with the earliest.
o: She completes her residency in family medicine
She opens the community clinic in Oakland
She graduates as a pharmacist
She works at a rural clinic in Nevada
She enters medical school
R.w: Pharmacy graduation (1979), medical school (1985), residency completed (1992), six years in Nevada (1992 to 1998), then the Oakland clinic (1998). The passage mentions the clinic first, but it happened last.

R.q:
(1) Our city should plant 5,000 street trees over the next five years. (2) A 2021 study by the state forestry office found that tree-lined blocks in our city were up to 9 °F cooler on summer afternoons than nearby blocks without trees. (3) Shade is a public health issue, not just a matter of looks. (4) During last July's heat wave, the county hospital treated 140 people for heat illness, most of them from neighborhoods with few trees. (5) Trees also make a neighborhood more pleasant for walking. (6) The council should fund the plan in this year's budget.

Which sentences present evidence rather than a claim or reason? Select all that apply.
o: Sentence 5
Sentence 4
Sentence 6
Sentence 2
Sentence 1
Sentence 3
R.w: Sentence 2 reports a study's measured temperature difference, and Sentence 4 reports hospital figures from a heat wave. Both are verifiable facts offered to support the claim.

n.0: Sentence 5 is an additional reason based on opinion; no evidence backs it up.
n.2: Sentence 6 is a call to action that restates the claim.
n.4: Sentence 1 is the main claim: what the author wants the city to do.
n.5: Sentence 3 is a reason stated as the author's judgment; the evidence for it comes in Sentence 4.

R.q: Read the passage. Select the sentence that best supports the inference that Marisol hides her uncertainty about the new medicine from the technician.

parts.t: Marisol reached the pharmacy counter ten minutes before closing.
She set three prescription bottles on the counter and lined them up by size.
The technician explained that her new tablet should be taken with food, and Marisol nodded quickly.
When he asked whether she had any questions, she said she was fine, but she kept turning the new bottle so that its label faced her.
Outside, she sat in her car and read the leaflet from start to finish before starting the engine.

sn.a: Marisol reached the pharmacy counter ten minutes before closing.
sn.b: She set three prescription bottles on the counter and lined them up by size.
sn.c: The technician explained that her new tablet should be taken with food, and Marisol nodded quickly.
sn.d: When he asked whether she had any questions, she said she was fine, but she kept turning the new bottle so that its label faced her.
sn.e: Outside, she sat in her car and read the leaflet from start to finish before starting the engine.

R.w: The inference has two parts: Marisol is unsure, and she keeps that from the technician. Sentence 4 shows both at once. She tells him she is fine, yet in front of him she keeps turning the bottle to reread its label.

n.a: Arriving just before closing may suggest she is rushed, but it says nothing about doubts over the medicine or about what she shows the technician.
n.b: Lining up the bottles suggests she is organized. It reveals neither uncertainty nor a gap between what she says and what she feels.
n.c: A quick nod signals understanding or agreement. On its own it fits a person who really did understand, so it does not show hidden uncertainty.
n.e: Reading the whole leaflet suggests she wanted more information, but it happens after she has left the counter, so it does not show her hiding anything from the technician.

R.q:
A health blogger claims that a 20-minute nap in mid-afternoon makes office workers more alert for the rest of the day. As evidence, she cites a poll of 300 of her readers: 82 percent of those who nap regularly said they feel sharper after a nap. She recommends that employers set aside quiet rooms where workers can sleep during their afternoon breaks.

Which of the following, if true, would most strengthen the blogger's claim?
o: Most of the blogger's readers who nap regularly say they enjoy taking naps.
Several famous inventors and leaders were known to take short daytime naps.
Workers who nap for an hour or more often report feeling groggy after waking.
Workers chosen at random to nap scored higher on alertness tests than non-nappers.
R.w: The blogger's evidence is a self-selected poll of how readers feel. A study that randomly assigns workers to nap and measures alertness with tests provides stronger, controlled evidence for the same claim.

n.0: Enjoying naps is not the same as being more alert, so this adds nothing to the claim.
n.1: Famous examples are anecdotes, not evidence that naps raise alertness in office workers.
n.2: This concerns long naps, not the 20-minute naps in the claim, and it does not show any benefit.

M.q: On a horizontal number line, point P is plotted at -2.6. Between which two consecutive integers is point P located?
o: -4 and -3
-3 and -2
2 and 3
-2 and -1
M.w: -2.6 is less than -2 and greater than -3 (-3 < -2.6 < -2), so P lies between -3 and -2, a little closer to -3.

n.0: -2.6 is greater than -3, so it lies to the right of -3.
n.2: This ignores the negative sign; 2.6 lies between 2 and 3.
n.3: -2.6 is less than -2, so it lies to the left of -2, not between -2 and -1.

M.q: A nurse measures a healing incision as 3 5/8 inches long and must record the length as a decimal in the electronic chart. Which decimal should be recorded?
M.w: Convert the fraction part: 5 ÷ 8 = 0.625. Add the whole number: 3 + 0.625 = 3.625.

n.0: 0.375 is the decimal for 3/8, not 5/8.
n.1: This writes the digits 5 and 8 after the decimal point instead of dividing 5 by 8.
n.2: This divides 8 by 5 (1.6) instead of 5 by 8, then adds 3.

M.q: A wound care kit contains enough gauze for 4 2/7 days of dressing changes. Which improper fraction is equal to 4 2/7?
M.w: Multiply the whole number by the denominator and add the numerator: 4 × 7 + 2 = 30. Keep the denominator: 30/7.

n.0: This multiplies the numerator by the denominator (2 × 7) and then adds the whole number (14 + 4 = 18).
n.1: This writes the digits 4 and 2 side by side as 42; 42/7 = 6, not 4 2/7.
n.3: This multiplies the whole number by the numerator (4 × 2) and then adds the denominator (8 + 7 = 15).

M.q: A dietitian estimates a man's resting calorie needs with the expression 10w + 6.25h - 5a + 5, where w is weight in kilograms, h is height in centimeters, and a is age in years. What value does the expression give for w = 80, h = 175, and a = 40?

n.1: This leaves off the constant + 5 at the end of the expression.
n.2: This adds 5a instead of subtracting it: the expression has - 5a, so 200 is taken away.
n.3: This treats the final + 5 as - 5, which makes the result 10 lower.

M.q: The number of doses, D, remaining in a multi-dose vial after t days of use is given by D = 40 - 3t. Which statement describes this relationship?
o: The vial starts with 40 doses and loses 3 doses per day
The vial starts with 3 doses and loses 40 doses per day
The vial starts with 40 doses and gains 3 doses per day
The vial starts with 37 doses and loses 3 doses per day
M.w: At t = 0, D = 40, the starting amount (y-intercept). The slope is -3, so D decreases by 3 for each day.

n.1: This swaps the intercept and the rate.
n.2: The coefficient of t is -3, a decrease, not a gain.
n.3: 37 is the amount left after 1 day; at t = 0 the vial holds 40.

M.q: A trail mix uses almonds, raisins, and cashews in the ratio 3:2:5 by weight. How many ounces of cashews are needed to make 4 pounds of trail mix? (1 pound = 16 ounces)
o: 12.8 ounces
20 ounces
19.2 ounces
32 ounces
M.w: 4 pounds = 4 × 16 = 64 ounces. Total parts = 3 + 2 + 5 = 10. Cashews = 5/10 × 64 = 32 ounces.

n.0: This is the raisin amount, 2/10 of 64 ounces; the ratio order is almonds, raisins, cashews.
n.1: This multiplies the cashew ratio term (5) by 4 pounds instead of finding 5/10 of 64 ounces.
n.2: This is the almond amount, 3/10 of 64 ounces; the ratio order is almonds, raisins, cashews.

M.q: A patient must take 2 tablets three times a day for 14 days and already has 25 of these tablets at home. More tablets are sold only in bottles of 30. How many bottles must be purchased to complete the full course?
o: 1 bottle
3 bottles
4 bottles
2 bottles
M.w: Tablets needed: 2 × 3 × 14 = 84. Subtract the 25 at home: 84 - 25 = 59. Bottles: 59 ÷ 30 = 1.97. One bottle is not enough, so round up to 2 bottles (60 tablets, enough for the 59 still needed).

n.0: 1 bottle rounds 1.97 down; 30 + 25 = 55 tablets would run out before the 84 needed.
n.1: 3 bottles ignores the 25 tablets at home (84 ÷ 30 = 2.8, rounded up), so it buys one bottle too many.
n.2: 4 bottles adds the 25 tablets at home to the 84 needed (109 ÷ 30 = 3.63) instead of subtracting them.

M.q: Jada and Luis split $1,260 in tutoring income. Jada receives $180 more than twice Luis's share. How much does Luis receive?
M.w: Let L = Luis's share, so Jada's is 2L + 180. Then L + 2L + 180 = 1,260, so 3L = 1,080 and L = $360. Jada gets 2(360) + 180 = $900; 360 + 900 = 1,260.

n.0: This is Jada's share, not Luis's.
n.1: This adds the $180 to $1,260 instead of subtracting it, giving 3L = 1,440.
n.3: This divides $1,080 by 2 instead of by 3. Luis's share counts once and Jada's contains it twice, so there are 3 shares.

M.q: The bar graph shows the number of patients seen by five hospital departments in one week. Select the department that saw exactly one-fourth of all the patients.
M.w: Total = 54 + 126 + 48 + 90 + 42 = 360. One-fourth of 360 = 90, which is Cardio.

n.b: 126 / 360 = 0.35, or 35%. ER has the largest share, which is more than one-fourth.

M.q: A 12-ounce bag of coffee makes 45 cups. At the same rate, how many cups can be made from a 32-ounce bag? Enter the number of cups.

tr.65: Added the 20-ounce difference to 45 instead of scaling.
tr.8.53: Set up the second ratio upside down (12 × 32 ÷ 45).

M.w: Set up 12/45 = 32/c. Cross-multiply: 12c = 1,440, so c = 120 cups.

M.q: A county health survey found that 48.7% of the 6,120 adults surveyed exercise at least three times a week. Which is the best estimate of the number of adults who exercise that often?
M.w: 48.7% is close to the benchmark 50% = 1/2, and 6,120 is close to 6,000. Estimate: 1/2 × 6,000 = 3,000. (Exact: about 2,980.)

n.0: 2,400 truncates 48.7% to 40% (0.4 × 6,000); 48.7% is much closer to 50%.
n.2: 3,500 rounds 6,120 up to 7,000 before halving; to the nearest thousand, 6,120 is 6,000.
n.3: 2,000 uses the benchmark 1/3, but 48.7% is much closer to 1/2.

M.q: A newborn weighs 3,400 grams at birth, and the parents ask for the weight in pounds. Use 1 kilogram = 2.2 pounds. What is the newborn's weight in pounds? Enter the number of pounds, rounded to the nearest tenth.

tr.7480: Multiplied 3,400 g by 2.2 without first converting grams to kilograms.
tr.1.5: Divided 3.4 kg by 2.2; kilograms to pounds means multiplying.
tr.7.4: Truncated 7.48 instead of rounding; the hundredths digit 8 rounds the tenths digit up.

M.q: A table shows the x-values 2, 5, and 8 paired with the y-values 7, 17.5, and 28. Which equation models the relationship shown in the table?
o: y = x + 5

n.0: This fits (2, 7) but gives 16, not 17.5, when x = 5.
n.2: This fits (2, 7) but gives 10, not 17.5, when x = 5.
n.3: This fits (2, 7) but gives 2.8 when x = 5; y increases as x increases, so it is not inverse.

M.q: A closed cylindrical can has a radius of 3 inches and a height of 8 inches. A paper label covers the curved side of the can but not the top or bottom. What is the area of the label? Use 3.14 for pi.
M.w: Unrolled, the label is a rectangle: circumference × height. Area = 2πrh = 2 × 3.14 × 3 × 8 = 150.72 in².

n.0: This uses πrh; the curved side's area is 2πrh (circumference × height).
n.1: 226.08 is the volume (πr²h) in cubic inches, not the label's area.
n.2: This adds the top and bottom circles (2 × 28.26 in²); the label covers the curved side.

M.q: A clinic waiting room has a circular rug with a diameter of 8 feet. The staff want to know how much floor space the rug covers. What is the area of the rug? Use 3.14 for pi.

n.0: 25.12 is the circumference (3.14 × 8), a length rather than an area.
n.2: This multiplies pi by the radius (3.14 × 4) instead of by the radius squared.
n.3: This uses the diameter (8 ft) as the radius; r = 8 ÷ 2 = 4 ft.

M.q: A lab assistant rounded each measurement to the nearest tenth. Select the rounded value that is incorrect.
M.w: To round to the nearest tenth, look only at the hundredths digit. In 4.649 the hundredths digit is 4, so the tenths digit stays the same: 4.6. Rounding first to 4.65 and then to 4.7 is a double-rounding error.

n.a: The hundredths digit of 0.96 is 6, so 0.9 rounds up to 1.0.
n.b: The hundredths digit is 4, so 3.449 rounds down to 3.4. The 9 in the thousandths place does not matter.
n.d: The hundredths digit is 5, so 7.05 rounds up to 7.1.
n.e: The hundredths digit is 4, so 12.348 rounds down to 12.3.
n.f: The hundredths digit is 5, so 2.951 rounds up, and 2.9 becomes 3.0.

M.q: Which value of n makes the equation 6n - 4(n - 2) = 30 true?
M.w: Distribute: 6n - 4n + 8 = 30. Combine like terms: 2n + 8 = 30. Subtract 8: 2n = 22. Divide by 2: n = 11. Check: 66 - 4(9) = 66 - 36 = 30.

n.0: This adds 6n and 4n instead of subtracting, giving 10n + 8 = 30.
n.2: This distributes the -4 to n only, giving 6n - 4n - 2 = 30, so 2n = 32.
n.3: Sign error: -4 × (-2) = +8, but this uses -8, giving 2n - 8 = 30.

M.q: A rectangular planter box holds 9 cubic feet of soil when filled to the top. The base of the box is 4 feet long and 1.5 feet wide. How deep is the planter box, in inches?
o: 18 in
1.5 in
27 in
15 in

n.1: 1.5 is the depth in feet; 1.5 ft × 12 = 18 in.
n.2: This divides by the length (9 ÷ 4 = 2.25 ft) but leaves out the width.
n.3: This treats 1.5 ft as 15 in, as if a foot had 10 inches; 1.5 ft = 18 in.

M.q: A nurse records the pulse rates of eight patients, in beats per minute: 72, 88, 64, 90, 76, 70, 84, 68. What is the median pulse rate?
M.w: Order the values: 64, 68, 70, 72, 76, 84, 88, 90. With 8 values, the median is the mean of the 4th and 5th: (72 + 76) / 2 = 74.

n.0: 612 / 8 = 76.5 is the mean, not the median.
n.1: 76 is only one of the two middle values; with an even count, average the two.
n.3: (90 + 76) / 2 = 83 takes the middle of the list as written, without ordering it first.

M.q: Marcus's phone plan costs $35 per month plus $0.10 for each text message over 200. His bill for March was $47.40. How many text messages did he send in March?
M.w: Let t = texts over 200: 35 + 0.10t = 47.40, so 0.10t = 12.40 and t = 124. Total texts sent = 200 + 124 = 324.

n.1: This subtracts the extra texts from 200 instead of adding them to 200.
n.2: This is the number of texts over the 200 included texts. The total sent is 200 + 124 = 324.
n.3: This divides the whole $47.40 bill by $0.10 without first removing the $35 monthly charge.

M.q: A large set of adult cholesterol levels is roughly symmetric and bell-shaped, with a mean of 190 mg/dL and a standard deviation of 20 mg/dL. Which statement is best supported?
o: About 68% of the levels fall between 170 and 210 mg/dL
About 95% of the levels fall between 170 and 210 mg/dL
About half of the levels are above 210 mg/dL
About 68% of the levels fall between 150 and 230 mg/dL
M.w: In a bell-shaped distribution, about 68% of values fall within 1 standard deviation of the mean: 190 - 20 = 170 to 190 + 20 = 210.

n.1: 170 to 210 is within 1 standard deviation, which holds about 68%, not 95%.
n.2: About half are above the mean of 190; only about 16% are above 210.
n.3: 150 to 230 is within 2 standard deviations, which holds about 95%, not 68%.

M.q: A dietitian compares the fraction of daily sodium in four meals: 45%, 0.5, 4/9 and 0.449. Which value is the least?
M.w: Convert each to a decimal: 45% = 0.450, 0.5 = 0.500, 4/9 = 0.444... and 0.449. Comparing digit by digit, 0.444... is the least, so 4/9 is the least.

n.0: 0.449 is greater than 4/9 = 0.444... (compare the thousandths: 9 > 4).
n.1: 0.5 is the greatest of the four values.
n.2: 45% = 0.45, which is greater than both 0.449 and 0.444...

M.q: A histogram shows weekly study hours for a class of nursing students: 0-4 hours, 3 students; 5-9 hours, 8 students; 10-14 hours, 12 students; 15-19 hours, 5 students; 20-24 hours, 2 students. What percent of the students studied at least 10 hours? Round to the nearest tenth and enter the number only.

tr.19: the number of students, not the percent
tr.36.7: the percent who studied fewer than 10 hours

M.q: Ava drove 168 miles to a nursing school open house in 3 hours 30 minutes. What was her average speed for the drive?
o: 42 miles per hour
50.9 miles per hour
56 miles per hour
48 miles per hour
M.w: 3 hours 30 minutes = 3.5 hours. Speed = distance ÷ time = 168 ÷ 3.5 = 48 miles per hour.

n.0: This rounds the time up to 4 hours before dividing.
n.1: This reads 3 hours 30 minutes as 3.30 hours. Thirty minutes is 0.5 hour, so the time is 3.5 hours.
n.2: This divides by 3 hours and ignores the extra 30 minutes.

M.q: A hospital shuttle drives between a clinic and the main hospital, a distance of 18 kilometers one way. The shuttle makes 5 round trips each day. Use 1 mile = 1.6 kilometers. How many miles does the shuttle drive each day?
o: 144 mi
288 mi
M.w: Round trip = 2 × 18 = 36 km; 5 round trips = 180 km. 180 ÷ 1.6 = 112.5 mi.

n.0: This counts 5 one-way trips; each round trip is 2 × 18 = 36 km.
n.2: This multiplies by 1.6 and also counts one-way trips (18 × 5 × 1.6).
n.3: This multiplies 180 km by 1.6; kilometers to miles means dividing by 1.6.

M.q: A clinic orders 24 boxes of exam gloves listed at $8.75 per box. The supplier takes $0.50 off the price of each box. What is the total cost of the order?
M.w: Discounted price per box: $8.75 - $0.50 = $8.25. Total: 24 × $8.25 = $198.00.

n.0: $209.50 takes $0.50 off the whole order instead of off each box.
n.2: $208.80 reads the discount as $0.05 per box ($8.70 × 24).
n.3: $210.00 is 24 × $8.75, the cost before the discount.

M.q: It takes 3 aides 8 hours to restock all of a hospital's supply rooms. Working at the same rate, how long would it take 4 aides to do the same job?
o: 10 hours 40 minutes
2 hours
7 hours
6 hours
M.w: This is an inverse proportion: aides × hours stays constant. 3 × 8 = 24 aide-hours, so 4 aides need 24 ÷ 4 = 6 hours.

n.0: This treats the relationship as direct. More aides finish faster, so the time must decrease.
n.1: This divides the original 8 hours by 4 aides and ignores that the 8 hours was for 3 aides.
n.2: This subtracts 1 hour for the 1 extra aide. The total work, 24 aide-hours, stays the same.

M.q: A taxi company sets the cost of a ride, C, based on the number of miles driven, m. Which statement correctly identifies the variables in this relationship?
o: C is independent, because it is the amount the rider pays
m is independent, and C depends on m
m is dependent, because it is measured during the ride
Both are dependent, because each changes with the other
M.w: The cost is calculated from the miles, so miles (m) is the input, or independent variable, and cost (C) is the output, or dependent variable.

n.0: The amount paid is the result of the miles driven, which makes C dependent.
n.2: Being measured does not make a variable dependent; m is the input that sets the cost.
n.3: One variable is the input and the other the output; C changes because m changes, not the reverse.

M.q: A delivery van can safely carry a load of no more than 1.5 tons. Each crate of medical supplies weighs 140 pounds. What is the greatest number of crates the van can carry on one trip?

n.0: This reads 1.5 tons as 1 ton 500 pounds (2,500 lb); 0.5 ton = 1,000 lb.
n.2: 3,000 ÷ 140 = 21.4, and 22 crates weigh 3,080 lb, which is over the limit, so round down.
n.3: This uses 1,000 pounds per ton; 1 ton = 2,000 lb.

M.q: Each row of the table pairs a fraction with a decimal or a percent. Select the value that is NOT equivalent to the fraction in its row.
M.w: 9/250 = 9 / 250 = 0.036 (or scale to thousandths: 9/250 = 36/1,000 = 0.036). The table shows 0.36, which is 10 times too large; 0.36 equals 9/25, not 9/250.

n.f: 1 / 125 = 0.008, and 0.008 x 100 = 0.8%. A percent below 1 looks wrong, but it is correct here.

M.q:
A stem-and-leaf plot shows the ages of patients seen at a clinic one morning (key: 3 | 1 = 31 years).
2 | 3 7 9
3 | 1 1 4 8
4 | 0 2 5 5 5 6
5 | 2 7
How many patients were older than 30 but younger than 45?
M.w: Ages greater than 30 and less than 45: 31, 31, 34, 38, 40, 42. That is 6 patients. The three 45s are not younger than 45.

n.0: 4 counts only the 3 stem (31, 31, 34, 38) and misses 40 and 42.
n.1: 9 includes the three patients aged 45, who are not younger than 45.
n.3: 10 counts every leaf on the 3 and 4 stems, including 45, 45, 45 and 46.

M.q: A nursing program received 450 applications this year and accepted 18% of the applicants. How many applicants did the program accept?
M.w: Part = percent × whole. 18% = 0.18, so 0.18 × 450 = 81 applicants.

n.1: This rounds 18% up to 20% before multiplying (0.20 × 450 = 90). Rounding is for estimating; the exact count uses 0.18.
n.2: This is the number of applicants who were not accepted (82%).
n.3: This divides 450 by 18 instead of multiplying 450 by 0.18.

M.q: Malik earns $17.50 per hour and worked 32 hours this week. 15% of his gross pay is withheld for taxes. From his take-home pay he pays $210 toward rent and $95 for groceries. How much of his take-home pay is left?

n.0: This subtracts the bills first and then takes 15% from what is left. Taxes are withheld from the full $560.
n.2: This is the take-home pay, an intermediate step; rent and groceries still have to be subtracted.
n.3: This subtracts rent and groceries from the gross pay of $560 and leaves out the 15% withheld for taxes.

M.q: Two clinics both have a mean wait time of 20 minutes. The standard deviation of the wait times is 3 minutes at Clinic A and 9 minutes at Clinic B. Which statement is correct?
o: Clinic B's wait times are more spread out around 20 minutes
Clinic B's patients wait longer on average than Clinic A's
Clinic A sees more patients, so its wait times vary less
Clinic A's median wait time is greater than Clinic B's
M.w: Standard deviation measures spread: roughly the typical distance of values from the mean. A larger SD (9 vs 3) means Clinic B's waits vary more around the shared mean of 20.

n.1: Both clinics have the same mean of 20 minutes; SD describes spread, not the average.
n.2: SD does not depend on the number of patients; nothing in the data gives patient counts.
n.3: Standard deviation gives no information about which median is larger.

M.q: A frequency table shows quiz scores for 20 students: a score of 6, 2 students; 7, 4 students; 8, 4 students; 9, 6 students; 10, 4 students. What is the median quiz score?
M.w: With 20 values, the median is the mean of the 10th and 11th. Running totals: 2, 6, 10, 16, 20. The 10th value is 8 and the 11th is 9, so the median is (8 + 9) / 2 = 8.5.

n.0: 166 / 20 = 8.3 is the mean, not the median.
n.1: 9 is the mode (6 students) and only the 11th value.
n.2: 8 is the middle of the score values 6 to 10 ignoring the frequencies, and it is only the 10th value.

M.q: A scrub top regularly priced at $48 is on sale for 35% off. A 6% sales tax is then charged on the sale price. What is the total cost of the scrub top? Round to the nearest cent.

n.0: This combines the rates into one change (35% off and 6% on = 29% off, 48 × 0.71). Tax is charged on the sale price, so the multipliers 0.65 and 1.06 must be applied in turn.
n.2: This writes 6% as 0.006 instead of 0.06, so the tax comes out as about 19 cents instead of $1.87.
n.3: This is the sale price before tax; the 6% sales tax still has to be added.

M.q: A researcher has recorded each of 40 adults' average daily calorie intake and their change in weight over one month. Which display best shows whether the two variables are related?
o: Line graph
Scatterplot
Double bar graph
Circle graph
M.w: A scatterplot plots one point per adult using two numeric variables, which shows whether they tend to rise or fall together.

n.0: A line graph tracks change over time, but these data pair two measurements for each person.
n.2: A double bar graph compares two series across categories, and 40 individual adults are not categories to compare.
n.3: A circle graph shows parts of a whole, not a relationship between two variables.

M.q: A closed rectangular box measures 10 inches long, 6 inches wide, and 4 inches high. How many square inches of wrapping paper are needed to cover the entire outside of the box with no overlap? Enter the number of square inches.

tr.124: Added the three different faces once; each face has a matching opposite face.
tr.240: Found the volume (10 × 6 × 4) instead of the surface area.

S.q: A cell-culture incubator's display reads 98.6 °F. A data logger in the same lab records temperature in kelvins. Enter the incubator temperature in kelvins, rounded to the nearest whole number.

tr.37: Converted to Celsius (37 °C) but stopped before adding 273.
tr.236: Converted to Celsius and then subtracted it from 273 instead of adding.
tr.372: Added 273 directly to the Fahrenheit reading (98.6 + 273 = 371.6) without converting to Celsius first.

S.q: Two sisters with the same parents differ genetically partly because segments were exchanged between homologous chromosomes while their parents' gametes formed. When does this exchange take place?
o: Metaphase of mitosis
Prophase II of meiosis
Anaphase I of meiosis
Prophase I of meiosis
S.w: Crossing over happens in prophase I, when homologous chromosomes pair up (synapsis) as tetrads and exchange segments.

n.0: Homologous chromosomes do not pair in mitosis, so there is no crossing over.
n.1: Homologs are no longer paired in prophase II, so crossing over between them does not occur then.
