n.2: Anaphase I is when homologs separate; the exchange had already happened in prophase I.

S.q: Propane burns according to the unbalanced equation C₃H₈ + O₂ → CO₂ + H₂O. When the equation is balanced using the smallest whole-number coefficients, what is the coefficient of O₂? Enter your answer as a whole number.

tr.4: Copied the coefficient of H₂O instead of counting the oxygen atoms needed.
tr.10: Gave the number of oxygen atoms instead of the number of O₂ molecules.

S.w: Balance C first: 3 C gives 3 CO₂. Balance H next: 8 H gives 4 H₂O. Count O on the right: 3 x 2 + 4 x 1 = 10 O atoms, which needs 10 / 2 = 5 O₂. Balanced: C₃H₈ + 5 O₂ → 3 CO₂ + 4 H₂O.

S.q: The panels show a dividing animal cell, out of order. Select the stage in which the centromeres split and sister chromatids are pulled toward opposite poles.
S.w: In anaphase the centromeres divide and spindle fibers pull the sister chromatids apart. Each chromatid, now a separate chromosome, moves toward an opposite pole, which is why the chromosomes in this panel are bent into V shapes as they are dragged away from the equator.

n.metaphase: In metaphase the chromosomes, each still two sister chromatids joined at the centromere, line up at the cell's equator. They have not yet separated.
n.prophase: In prophase chromatin condenses into visible chromosomes and the spindle forms. The sister chromatids are still joined.
n.telophase: In telophase the separated chromosomes have already reached the poles and nuclear envelopes re-form around them.
n.interphase: Interphase is not part of mitosis. DNA is replicated during its S phase, creating the sister chromatids that separate later.

S.q: A spirometry report lists a vital capacity of 4,800 mL and a residual volume of 1,200 mL. What is this person's total lung capacity?
S.w: Total lung capacity = vital capacity + residual volume = 4,800 + 1,200 = 6,000 mL.

n.0: 4,800 mL is the vital capacity; it leaves out the residual volume that is always in the lungs.
n.1: 5,300 mL adds a 500 mL tidal volume, which is already included in vital capacity.
n.2: 3,600 mL subtracts residual volume instead of adding it.

S.q: Which of the following joints are correctly matched with their type of synovial joint? Select all that apply.
o: Knee: hinge
Thumb carpometacarpal: saddle
Atlantoaxial (C1-C2): pivot
Wrist (radiocarpal): ball-and-socket
Elbow (humeroulnar): pivot
Hip: condyloid
S.w: The knee is a (modified) hinge joint, the atlantoaxial joint between C1 and C2 is a pivot joint that rotates the head, and the thumb carpometacarpal joint is the classic saddle joint.

n.3: The radiocarpal (wrist) joint is condyloid (ellipsoid) and biaxial; the ball-and-socket joints are the shoulder and hip.
n.4: The humeroulnar joint is a hinge; the pivot joint at the elbow is the proximal radioulnar joint.
n.5: The hip is a ball-and-socket joint; condyloid joints include the wrist and the knuckles.

S.q: After ovulation, the fimbriae sweep the secondary oocyte into the uterine tube. In a typical pregnancy, where does fertilization of the oocyte take place?
o: In the ampulla of the uterine tube
In the ruptured follicle of the ovary
In the functional layer of the endometrium
In the cervical canal of the uterus
S.w: Fertilization usually occurs in the ampulla, the wide outer portion of the uterine tube. Cilia and peristalsis then move the developing embryo to the uterus, where it implants in the endometrium.

n.1: The oocyte leaves the ovary at ovulation; the ruptured follicle then becomes the corpus luteum.
n.2: The endometrium is where the blastocyst implants about a week later, not where fertilization occurs.
n.3: Sperm pass through the cervix on the way up; fertilization happens farther along, in the uterine tube.

S.q: A pharmacy technician sorts four samples on a shelf. Which of these samples is a homogeneous mixture?
o: Oil and vinegar dressing
Distilled water
Sand stirred into water
Salt dissolved in water
S.w: Salt water is a solution, a homogeneous mixture: the dissolved salt is spread evenly, so every part has the same composition, and the proportions can vary.

n.0: Oil and vinegar separate into visible layers, so the dressing is a heterogeneous mixture.
n.1: Distilled water is a pure substance, the compound H₂O, not a mixture.
n.2: Sand does not dissolve and settles out, so sand in water is a heterogeneous mixture (a suspension).

S.q: In a class discussion about how science works, a student asks how a scientific law differs from a scientific theory. Which statement gives the correct distinction?
o: A law explains why an event happens; a theory describes the pattern.
A theory becomes a law once enough experiments have proven it correct.
A theory is an educated guess that scientists have not yet tested.
A law describes what consistently happens; a theory explains why.
S.w: A law describes a consistent pattern, often mathematically (conservation of mass), without explaining it. A theory is a broad, well-tested explanation of many observations (cell theory). They do different jobs, so theories do not turn into laws.

n.0: This swaps the roles: laws describe, and theories explain.
n.1: Theories do not graduate into laws; a well-supported theory stays a theory because it explains rather than describes.
n.2: That describes a hypothesis; a theory is supported by extensive, repeated testing.

S.q: After a fall, Diego has damage confined to his cerebellum. Which problem is he most likely to show during his recovery?
o: Loss of control of breathing rhythm
Inability to understand spoken language
Loss of balance and poorly coordinated movement
Inability to regulate body temperature and thirst
S.w: The cerebellum coordinates movement and controls balance and posture, so damage to it produces unsteady, poorly coordinated movement.

n.0: Breathing rhythm is set by the medulla oblongata, with help from the pons, not the cerebellum.
n.1: Understanding spoken language depends on Wernicke's area in the temporal lobe.
n.3: Body temperature and thirst are regulated by the hypothalamus.

S.q: In anatomical position, which pairing correctly describes where the radius lies in the forearm and where the tibia lies in the leg?
o: Radius lateral; tibia lateral
Radius lateral; tibia medial
Radius medial; tibia medial
Radius medial; tibia lateral
S.w: In anatomical position (palms forward) the radius is on the lateral, thumb side of the forearm and the ulna is medial. In the leg the large, weight-bearing tibia is medial and the thin fibula is lateral.

n.0: The tibia is medial; the lateral leg bone is the fibula.
n.2: The radius is lateral; the medial forearm bone is the ulna.
n.3: Both are reversed: the ulna is the medial forearm bone and the fibula is the lateral leg bone.

S.q: A biology tutor writes four statements on the board comparing prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells. Which of the statements is accurate?
o: Prokaryotes divide by mitosis and eukaryotes by binary fission.
Prokaryotic DNA is linear and eukaryotic DNA is one circular loop.
Bacteria have peptidoglycan walls and plants have cellulose walls.
Prokaryotic ribosomes are 80S and eukaryotic ribosomes are 70S.
S.w: Bacteria (prokaryotes) build their cell walls from peptidoglycan, and plants (eukaryotes) build theirs from cellulose. Each of the other statements reverses a real difference: ribosome size (prokaryotes 70S, eukaryotes 80S), method of division and form of the DNA.

n.0: This reverses the methods: prokaryotes divide by binary fission and eukaryotes use mitosis or meiosis.
n.1: This reverses the DNA forms: prokaryotes usually have one circular chromosome and eukaryotes have several linear chromosomes.
n.3: This reverses the sizes: prokaryotes have smaller 70S ribosomes and eukaryotes have 80S ribosomes.

S.q: In a drug trial, doses of 10, 20 and 30 mg lowered systolic blood pressure by 5, 10 and 15 mmHg. A student predicts that a 90 mg dose would lower it by 45 mmHg. How should this prediction be evaluated?
o: It extends the trend far past the doses tested, so it is unreliable.
It is reliable, because it lies within the range of the data collected.
It is reliable, because the three data points form a straight line.
It is too low, because drug effects grow exponentially with the dose.
S.w: Predicting beyond the range tested (extrapolation) is unreliable: the trend may level off or reverse at higher doses. The data cover only 10 to 30 mg, so 90 mg is far outside them.

n.1: 90 mg is far outside the tested range of 10 to 30 mg, so the prediction is an extrapolation.
n.2: A straight line within the tested range does not show the trend continues three times beyond it.
n.3: The data rise by a steady 5 mmHg per 10 mg; nothing in them suggests exponential growth.

S.q: Red blood cells are placed in a salt solution that has a higher solute concentration than the fluid inside the cells. What happens to the cells?
o: Salt moves into the cells until they burst
Water moves out of the cells, and they shrink
Water moves both ways equally, and size holds
Water moves into the cells, and they swell
S.w: In osmosis, water moves across a semipermeable membrane toward the higher solute concentration. The outside solution is hypertonic, so water leaves the cells and they shrink (crenate).

n.0: Osmosis is the movement of water, not salt; the cells lose water and shrink.
n.2: Equal movement both ways describes an isotonic solution, such as 0.9% saline.
n.3: Swelling happens in a hypotonic solution, where the outside solute concentration is lower.

S.q: The pancreas releases digestive enzymes through a duct into the small intestine and also releases insulin directly into the bloodstream. Which classification of the pancreas is correct?
o: An endocrine gland, because its enzymes act as hormones in the blood
Both an exocrine and an endocrine gland, with ducted and ductless parts
An exocrine gland, because insulin also leaves the gland through a duct
An endocrine gland, because a gland making any hormone is endocrine
S.w: Exocrine glands secrete through ducts onto a surface (the pancreatic enzymes), and endocrine glands are ductless and secrete hormones into the blood (insulin). The pancreas does both.

n.0: Digestive enzymes travel through a duct to the small intestine; they are exocrine secretions, not hormones.
n.2: Insulin is a hormone released directly into the blood without a duct, which is an endocrine function.
n.3: Making a hormone shows endocrine function, but the pancreas also secretes enzymes through a duct, so it is exocrine as well.

S.q: Compared with veins, which features are typical of arteries? Select all that apply.
o: Higher internal pressure and a palpable pulse
Valves that prevent backflow in the limbs
Thicker walls with more smooth muscle and elastic tissue
A wall made of a single endothelial layer
A larger lumen that holds most of the blood at rest
S.w: Arteries have thick walls with more smooth muscle and elastic tissue to withstand and smooth the high pressure from the ventricles, which is felt as a pulse.

n.1: Valves are a feature of veins, especially in the legs.
n.3: A single endothelial layer describes capillaries.
n.4: Veins have the larger lumens and hold about 60-70% of blood volume at rest.

S.q: The heart is shown in anatomical position. Select the chamber whose wall is thickest because its contraction must drive blood through the entire systemic circulation.
S.w: The left ventricle pumps oxygenated blood through the aortic valve into the aorta and on to every systemic tissue, against far more resistance than the lungs offer. It therefore has the thickest myocardium and generates the highest pressure. In anatomical position the patient's left is the viewer's right, so it is the lower chamber on the viewer's right.

n.rv: The right ventricle pumps only to the nearby, low-resistance lungs, so its wall is much thinner. It sits on the viewer's left in anatomical position; choosing it is the mirror-image error.
n.la: The left atrium receives oxygenated blood from the pulmonary veins and only tops up ventricular filling, so its wall is thin.
n.ra: The right atrium receives deoxygenated blood from the venae cavae. Atria are thin-walled receiving chambers.

S.q: A sample of bacteria from a patient's wound is Gram stained and appears purple under the microscope. What does this result indicate about the bacteria?
o: Gram-negative, with an outer lipid membrane
Gram-negative, with a thick peptidoglycan wall
Gram-positive, with a thin wall and outer membrane
Gram-positive, with a thick peptidoglycan wall
S.w: Gram-positive bacteria have a thick peptidoglycan wall that holds the purple (violet) stain. Gram-negative bacteria have a thin wall plus an outer membrane and stain pink or red.

n.0: An outer membrane is the Gram-negative feature, and those bacteria stain pink, not purple.
n.1: Gram-negative bacteria stain pink and have a thin peptidoglycan layer, not a thick one.
n.2: A thin wall with an outer membrane is the Gram-negative structure, which does not stain purple.

S.q: A college student with a common cold caused by a rhinovirus asks a clinic nurse for an antibiotic. Which statement best explains why an antibiotic will not help?
o: Viruses are not cells and lack the targets antibiotics act on.
Viruses are prokaryotic cells whose walls block antibiotics.
Rhinoviruses multiply too fast for antibiotics to act.
Rhinoviruses are bacteria that have become drug resistant.
S.w: Antibiotics kill or inhibit bacteria by acting on bacterial structures and processes. Viruses are not cells (no cell wall, ribosomes or metabolism of their own), so antibiotics have no effect on them.

n.1: Viruses are not cells at all, prokaryotic or otherwise, and they have no cell wall.
n.2: Speed of replication is not the problem. Antibiotics have no bacterial target to act on in a virus, however slowly it multiplies.
n.3: Rhinoviruses are viruses, not bacteria, so antibiotic resistance does not apply to them.

S.q: A student is listing the typical properties of acids for a study guide. Which properties are characteristic of acids? Select all that apply.
o: They react with zinc to release hydrogen gas
They turn blue litmus paper red
They taste sour
They turn phenolphthalein pink
They accept protons from water molecules
They feel slippery to the touch
S.w: Acids taste sour, turn blue litmus red, and react with active metals such as zinc to release hydrogen gas (H₂). They donate protons (H+).

n.3: Phenolphthalein turns pink in bases; it stays colorless in acids.
n.4: Accepting protons defines a Bronsted-Lowry base; acids donate protons.
n.5: A slippery, soapy feel is a property of bases.

S.q: Which layer of the epidermis is the deepest and contains the dividing stem cells that replace the cells continually shed from the skin surface?
o: Stratum spinosum
Stratum corneum
Stratum basale
Stratum granulosum
S.w: The stratum basale (germinativum) is the deepest epidermal layer: a single row of dividing stem cells that push new keratinocytes upward. It also holds melanocytes and Merkel cells.

n.0: The stratum spinosum lies just above the basale and contains Langerhans cells; it is not the deepest layer.
n.1: The stratum corneum is the most superficial layer of dead, flattened, keratin-filled cells.
n.3: The stratum granulosum is a middle layer where keratinization advances and cells begin to die.

S.q: Shortly after Jamal eats a large pasta dinner, his blood glucose rises. Which hormone does his pancreas release in response, and from which cells?
o: Glucagon, from pancreatic alpha cells
Insulin, from pancreatic beta cells
Insulin, from pancreatic alpha cells
Glucagon, from pancreatic beta cells
S.w: High blood glucose after a meal triggers the beta cells of the pancreatic islets to release insulin, which lowers glucose by moving it into cells and storing it as glycogen.

n.0: Glucagon raises blood glucose, so it is released when glucose is low, not after a meal.
n.2: Insulin is the right hormone, but it comes from beta cells; alpha cells make glucagon.
n.3: Glucagon raises blood glucose and is made by alpha cells, so both parts are wrong.

S.q: When phospholipids are placed in water, they arrange themselves into a double layer. Which feature of phospholipid structure explains this arrangement?
o: Their tails are polar and are attracted to the surrounding water.
Their hydrophilic heads face water while hydrophobic tails face inward.
Their three fatty acid tails make them dissolve in water.
Their nonpolar heads face water while polar tails face inward.
S.w: A phospholipid has a hydrophilic (polar) phosphate head and two hydrophobic (nonpolar) fatty acid tails. In water the heads face outward and the tails hide inside, forming a bilayer.

n.0: The fatty acid tails are nonpolar and hydrophobic, so they avoid water.
n.2: Phospholipids have two fatty acid tails (triglycerides have three), and the tails repel water.
n.3: Polarity is reversed: the heads are polar and the tails are nonpolar.

S.q: Lymph collected from the left arm, the abdomen and both legs must return to the bloodstream. By which route does this lymph re-enter the blood?
o: Thoracic duct into the left subclavian vein
Right lymphatic duct into the right subclavian vein
Thoracic duct into the right subclavian vein
Thoracic duct into the superior vena cava
S.w: The thoracic duct drains most of the body, including both legs, the abdomen and the left arm, into the left subclavian vein. The right lymphatic duct drains the right arm and the right side of the head and thorax.

n.1: The right lymphatic duct drains the right arm and the right side of the head and thorax, not the left arm or the legs.
n.2: The thoracic duct joins the venous system on the left side, at the left subclavian vein.
n.3: The thoracic duct empties into the left subclavian vein, not directly into the superior vena cava.

S.q: A short segment of double-stranded DNA contains 4 guanine-cytosine pairs and 6 adenine-thymine pairs. How many hydrogen bonds hold its two strands together?
S.w: Step 1: G-C pairs have 3 hydrogen bonds and A-T pairs have 2. Step 2: (4 x 3) + (6 x 2) = 12 + 12 = 24.

n.0: 30 counts every pair as having 3 hydrogen bonds; A-T pairs have 2.
n.1: 20 counts every pair as having 2 hydrogen bonds; G-C pairs have 3.
n.3: 26 swaps the bond numbers: (4 x 2) + (6 x 3) gives 26.

S.q: A lab report lists a healthy adult's red blood cell count as 5.2 × 10⁶ cells per microliter of blood. How is this count written in standard form?
o: 520,000 cells
S.w: A positive exponent of 6 moves the decimal point 6 places to the right: 5.2 becomes 5,200,000.

n.0: This moves the decimal point 5 places (5.2 × 10⁵).
n.1: This moves the decimal point 7 places (5.2 × 10⁷).
n.2: This treats the exponent as negative and moves the decimal point to the left.

S.q: Which pairing of an accessory digestive organ with something it secretes into the digestive tract is correct?
o: Salivary glands: pepsinogen
Gallbladder: bile that it produces
Pancreas: bicarbonate and lipase
Liver: trypsin and chymotrypsin
S.w: The exocrine pancreas releases pancreatic juice containing bicarbonate (to neutralize acid chyme) and enzymes such as lipase, amylase, trypsinogen and nucleases.

n.0: Pepsinogen is made by chief cells in the stomach; saliva contains amylase and lingual lipase.
n.1: The gallbladder stores and concentrates bile, but the liver produces it.
n.3: Trypsin and chymotrypsin are pancreatic enzymes; the liver makes bile, not digestive enzymes.

S.q: Which statements about the hormonal control of the testes are correct? Select all that apply.
o: FSH and testosterone together stimulate spermatogenesis via Sertoli cells.
FSH from the posterior pituitary acts on the Sertoli cells.
Testosterone raises GnRH output by positive feedback on the hypothalamus.
LH stimulates interstitial (Leydig) cells to secrete testosterone.
Leydig cells line the seminiferous tubules and nourish developing sperm.
Sertoli cells secrete inhibin, which suppresses FSH release.
S.w: LH acts on Leydig cells, which secrete testosterone. FSH, together with testosterone, acts through the Sertoli cells to drive spermatogenesis. Sertoli cells secrete inhibin, which suppresses FSH.

n.1: FSH is released by the anterior pituitary, not the posterior pituitary.
n.2: Testosterone exerts negative feedback on the hypothalamus and pituitary, lowering GnRH and LH.
n.4: Sertoli cells, not Leydig cells, line the tubules and nourish developing sperm; Leydig cells sit between the tubules.

S.q: A study of 400 healthy men aged 20 to 30 finds that a daily supplement lowered their resting heart rate. Which conclusion is best supported by this study?
o: The supplement lowers resting heart rate in adults of any age.
The supplement lowers resting heart rate in women aged 60 to 70.
The supplement will lower heart rate in patients with heart disease.
The supplement lowered heart rate in the healthy young men studied.
S.w: Sound conclusions stay within the population and conditions tested. The study included only healthy men aged 20 to 30.

n.0: Adults of other ages and sexes were not tested; the result cannot be extended to them.
n.1: Older women were not studied, so this generalizes beyond the tested population.
n.2: Only healthy men took part, so the effect in heart patients is unknown.

S.q: A nurse records a patient's body temperature every 2 hours for 24 hours and wants to show the class how it changed across the day. Which type of graph is the best choice?
o: Histogram
Circle graph
Line graph
Bar graph
S.w: A line graph shows how a continuous variable (temperature) changes over time, with time on the x-axis.

n.0: A histogram shows how often values fall in each interval, which loses the order of the readings in time.
n.1: A circle (pie) graph shows parts of a whole that add to 100%, not change over time.
n.3: A bar graph compares separate categories; it hides the continuous trend between readings.

S.q: A sealed container of nitrogen gas is warmed from 20 °C to 40 °C. Which quantity does the temperature reading of the gas directly measure?
o: The number of particle collisions in one second
The potential energy stored between particles
The average kinetic energy of the gas particles
The total heat energy stored in the whole sample
S.w: Temperature is a measure of the average kinetic energy of the particles in a sample. Warming the gas makes its particles move faster on average.

n.0: Collision frequency rises with temperature, but it is a result of faster motion, not what temperature measures.
n.1: Potential energy between particles changes during phase changes, while temperature stays constant; temperature tracks kinetic energy.
n.3: Total heat energy depends on the amount of substance as well as the temperature; temperature measures the average energy per particle.

S.q: A nurse asks a patient to raise the arm out to the side until it is level with the shoulder. Which muscle is the prime mover for this abduction of the arm?
o: Pectoralis major
Latissimus dorsi
Trapezius
Deltoid
S.w: The deltoid, which caps the shoulder, is the prime mover of arm abduction (moving the arm away from the midline). It is also a common intramuscular injection site.

n.0: The pectoralis major flexes, adducts and medially rotates the arm.
n.1: The latissimus dorsi extends and adducts the arm, the opposite direction to abduction.
n.2: The trapezius elevates and retracts the scapula and extends the head; it does not abduct the arm at the shoulder joint.

S.q: Signals from the eyes, ears, taste buds and skin pass through one structure in the diencephalon before reaching the cerebral cortex. Which structure is this?
o: Corpus callosum
Hypothalamus
Thalamus
Pons
S.w: The thalamus is the relay station that sends sensory information on to the cerebral cortex. Smell is the one sense not relayed through it first.

n.0: The corpus callosum connects the two cerebral hemispheres; it does not relay incoming sensory signals to the cortex.
n.1: The hypothalamus regulates homeostasis and controls the pituitary gland; it is not the main sensory relay.
n.3: The pons is part of the brainstem; it relays signals between the cerebrum and cerebellum and helps regulate breathing.

S.q: A double-stranded DNA fragment contains 400 bases in total, and 120 of them are cytosine. How many of the bases are adenine? Enter a whole number.

tr.160: found A + T but did not halve it

S.w: Step 1: C = G, so there are 120 guanine as well, and G + C = 240. Step 2: A + T = 400 - 240 = 160. Step 3: A = T, so adenine = 160 / 2 = 80.

S.q: A student measures the density of an aluminum block as 2.43 g/cm³. The accepted value is 2.70 g/cm³. Enter the percent error as a whole number.

tr.11: Divided by the measured value (0.27 / 2.43) instead of the accepted value.
tr.27: Used the difference (0.27) times 100 without dividing by the accepted value.
tr.90: Divided the measured value by the accepted value (2.43 / 2.70) without finding the difference.

S.w: Percent error = |measured - accepted| / accepted x 100% = |2.43 - 2.70| / 2.70 x 100% = 0.27 / 2.70 x 100% = 10%.

S.q: A glowing wooden splint smolders slowly in air, but when it is placed in a jar of pure oxygen, it bursts into flame. Which factor best explains the faster reaction in pure oxygen?
o: A higher concentration of one of the reactants
A larger surface area of the wood exposed in the jar
A lower activation energy for oxygen in a closed jar
A catalyst present in pure oxygen but missing in air
S.w: Air is only about 21% oxygen. In pure oxygen, there are many more O₂ molecules per unit volume, so they collide with the wood far more often. Raising the concentration of a reactant increases the reaction rate.

n.1: The splint is the same piece of wood in both cases, so its surface area has not changed.
n.2: Activation energy is a property of the reaction pathway; it changes when a catalyst is added, not when oxygen is concentrated.
n.3: Oxygen is a reactant in combustion, not a catalyst, and the rate rises because there is more of it.

S.q: During a hard cough or a forced exhalation, which muscles contract to push air out of the lungs?
o: The external intercostals and the diaphragm
The external intercostals and abdominal muscles
The diaphragm and the internal intercostals
The internal intercostals and abdominal muscles
S.w: Forced expiration is active: the internal intercostals pull the ribs down and the abdominal muscles push the abdominal organs up against the relaxed diaphragm, shrinking the thorax.

n.0: The external intercostals and diaphragm are the muscles of inspiration.
n.1: The abdominal muscles help, but the external intercostals lift the ribs for inspiration.
n.2: The internal intercostals help, but the diaphragm relaxes during expiration; contraction would enlarge the thorax.

S.q: An atom of iron-56 has an atomic number of 26. How many neutrons are in the nucleus of this atom? Enter your answer as a whole number.

tr.26: Gave the number of protons (the atomic number) instead of neutrons.
tr.56: Gave the mass number, which counts protons and neutrons together.
tr.82: Added the mass number and atomic number instead of subtracting.

S.w: Mass number = protons + neutrons, so neutrons = mass number - atomic number = 56 - 26 = 30.

S.q: Chlorine has atomic number 17. In a neutral chlorine atom, how many electrons occupy the outermost (third) electron shell? Enter your answer as a whole number.

tr.1: Counted the electrons chlorine needs to gain, not the electrons it has.
tr.8: Assumed the outer shell is a full octet; chlorine is one electron short of 8.
tr.17: Gave the total number of electrons, not the outer-shell count.

S.w: Fill shells from the inside: first shell 2, second shell 8, which uses 10 electrons. The remaining 17 - 2 - 8 = 7 electrons are in the third shell (arrangement 2, 8, 7), matching chlorine's place in group 17.

S.q: A nursing student moves from a coastal city to a mountain town about 2,500 m above sea level. What should she predict about the boiling point of water when she cooks pasta there?
o: Higher, because the air pressure is higher
Higher, because the air pressure is lower
Lower, because the air pressure is lower
Lower, because the air pressure is higher
S.w: Air pressure falls as altitude rises (an inverse relationship). Water boils when its vapor pressure matches the air pressure, so lower air pressure means water boils at a lower temperature.

n.0: Air pressure is lower, not higher, at altitude, and higher pressure would raise the boiling point.
n.1: Lower air pressure lowers the boiling point; the direction of the effect is reversed.
n.3: The boiling point is lower, but because air pressure decreases with altitude, not increases.

S.q: When solutions of silver nitrate and sodium chloride are mixed, a white solid forms: AgNO₃ + NaCl → AgCl + NaNO₃. How is this reaction best classified?
o: Synthesis, forming one new solid product
Decomposition, splitting into two products
Double replacement, forming a precipitate
Single replacement, forming a precipitate
S.w: The two compounds exchange partners (AB + CD → AD + CB): silver pairs with chloride and sodium pairs with nitrate. The insoluble AgCl appears as a white precipitate.

n.0: Synthesis gives a single product; this reaction gives two (AgCl and NaNO₃).
n.1: Decomposition starts with one compound breaking apart; here two compounds react.
n.3: A precipitate does form, but both reactants are compounds that swap ions, so it is double, not single, replacement.

S.q: A nursing student investigates whether two hand sanitizers differ in how well they reduce bacteria on skin. Place her actions in the order they occur in the scientific method, starting with the first.
o: Reads published studies on alcohol-based sanitizers
Swabs hands after each sanitizer and incubates the plates
Concludes whether the data support her prediction
Counts colonies on each plate and compares the means
Predicts that the 70% alcohol gel will leave fewer bacteria
Presents her method and results to classmates for review
S.w: Background research comes first, then the hypothesis (her prediction), then the experiment (swabbing and incubating), then data analysis (counting and comparing), then the conclusion, and finally communicating results for review.

S.q: A city health report shows that in months when ice-cream sales are high, clinics also treat more sunburns. Which explanation is most scientifically sound?
o: Eating ice cream may make the skin more prone to burning.
Hot, sunny weather likely drives both of the increases.
The pattern shows one of the two causes the other.
Sunburn pain may lead people to buy more ice cream.
S.w: Correlation does not prove causation. A third (confounding) variable, hot sunny weather, plausibly raises both ice-cream sales and sun exposure.

n.0: This assumes causation from a correlation with no controlled evidence.
n.2: Two variables rising together can share a third cause, so the pattern does not show that either causes the other.
n.3: This reverses the direction of cause, which a correlation alone cannot establish either.

S.q: A women's health clinic leaflet notes that urinary tract infections are more common in females than in males. Which anatomical difference best explains this?
o: The female urethra is longer, so urine pools in it between voids
The female ureters are shorter, so bacteria reach the kidneys sooner
The female urethra is shorter, so bacteria reach the bladder sooner
The female urethra carries both urine and reproductive fluids
S.w: The female urethra is about 4 cm long, compared with about 20 cm in males, so bacteria from outside have a shorter route to the bladder.

n.0: The female urethra is shorter (about 4 cm) than the male urethra (about 20 cm), not longer.
n.1: The key difference is the urethra, not the ureters; bacteria enter from outside through the urethra and reach the bladder first.
n.3: Carrying both urine and semen describes the male urethra; the female urethra carries only urine.

S.q: A lab analysis shows that an unknown macromolecule from a cell contains carbon, hydrogen, oxygen and nitrogen, but no phosphorus. Which type of macromolecule is it most likely to be?
o: A nucleic acid
A protein
A carbohydrate
A phospholipid
S.w: Step 1: nitrogen rules out carbohydrates and simple fats. Step 2: the absence of phosphorus rules out nucleic acids and phospholipids, leaving protein (C, H, O, N, often S).

n.0: Nucleic acids contain phosphorus in their phosphate groups.
n.2: Common carbohydrates such as sugars, starch and glycogen contain only C, H and O, so nitrogen points away from them.
n.3: Phospholipids contain a phosphate group, so phosphorus would be present.

S.q: This frontal section is from an adult femur. Select the structure made of a connective tissue that has no blood vessels of its own and relies on diffusion from surrounding fluid for its nutrients.
S.w: Articular cartilage is hyaline cartilage covering the joint surface of the epiphysis. Cartilage is the classic avascular connective tissue: its cells receive nutrients by diffusion from synovial fluid, which is why it heals slowly. Most other connective tissues, bone included, are vascular.

n.periosteum: The periosteum is a vascular membrane of dense connective tissue. Its blood vessels and nerves supply the bone and support growth in width and repair.
n.compact: Compact bone is vascular: the central canal of each osteon carries blood vessels and nerves.
n.spongy: Spongy bone is vascular. The spaces between its trabeculae hold red marrow with a rich blood supply.
n.epi_line: The growth plate of a child is avascular hyaline cartilage, but in an adult it has ossified. The epiphyseal line is bone, not cartilage.
n.medullary: In an adult the medullary cavity holds yellow marrow (fat), supplied by vessels entering through the nutrient foramen. It is not cartilage.

S.q: A student is summarizing the structure of the epidermis for a study guide. Which statements about the epidermis are accurate? Select all that apply.
o: Its melanocytes lie mainly in the stratum corneum
It is stratified squamous epithelium
It is avascular
Most of its cells are keratinocytes
It is built mainly of collagen and elastin
Its deepest layer is the stratum corneum
S.w: The epidermis is keratinized stratified squamous epithelium with no blood vessels of its own (it is nourished from the dermis). Keratinocytes are its most numerous cells.

n.0: Melanocytes lie in the stratum basale, the deepest layer.
n.4: Collagen and elastin fibers are features of the dermis, which is connective tissue.
n.5: The stratum corneum is the most superficial layer; the deepest is the stratum basale.

S.q: For a gene with complete dominance, A is dominant over a. Which crosses can produce offspring showing the recessive phenotype? Select all that apply.
o: aa x aa
AA x AA
AA x aa
Aa x aa
AA x Aa
Aa x Aa
S.w: A recessive phenotype needs aa, so each parent must be able to pass on a. Aa x Aa (1/4 aa), Aa x aa (1/2 aa) and aa x aa (all aa) can all produce it.

n.1: AA x AA gives only AA offspring.
n.2: AA x aa gives only Aa offspring, all showing the dominant phenotype.
n.4: AA x Aa gives AA and Aa offspring; the AA parent always passes on A.

S.q: Which of the following structures is made of smooth muscle?
o: Myocardium
Arrector pili
Muscles of facial expression
Diaphragm
S.w: The arrector pili are small bundles of smooth muscle attached to hair follicles; their contraction makes hairs stand up (goosebumps). Other smooth muscle sites include blood vessels, airways, the iris and hollow organs.

n.0: The myocardium is cardiac muscle: involuntary like smooth muscle, but striated, with branched cells joined by intercalated discs.
n.2: Muscles of facial expression are striated, voluntary skeletal muscles, even though many insert into the skin rather than onto bone.
n.3: The diaphragm is skeletal muscle; it contracts automatically during quiet breathing but is striated and can be controlled voluntarily.

S.q: Pancreatic juice contains enzymes for each major class of nutrient. Which enzyme in pancreatic juice breaks down the DNA and RNA found in food?
o: Chymotrypsin
Maltase
Peptidase
Nuclease
S.w: Pancreatic nucleases digest nucleic acids into nucleotides, which are broken into sugars, bases and phosphate and absorbed into the blood.

n.0: Chymotrypsin is a pancreatic enzyme, but it digests proteins.
n.1: Maltase is a brush-border enzyme that splits the sugar maltose.
n.2: Peptidases are brush-border enzymes that finish protein digestion.

E.q: A nurse is writing a reference letter for a former nursing aide: "Ms. Alvarez was ___ about following every infection-control step." Which word completes the sentence with the most positive connotation?
o: persnickety
obsessive
meticulous
nitpicky
E.w: All four words describe close attention to detail, but only "meticulous" has a positive, professional connotation.

n.0: "Persnickety" is informal and suggests fussing over trivial details, a negative connotation.
n.1: "Obsessive" suggests an unhealthy fixation, a negative connotation in a reference letter.
n.3: "Nitpicky" is informal and suggests petty fault-finding, a negative connotation.

E.q: Original: "Patients who walk within 24 hours after surgery tend to recover faster." A student writes, "Getting patients walking within a day of surgery tends to speed their recovery," with no citation. Which statement is correct?
o: It is plagiarism, since the borrowed idea is not credited
It is patchwriting, since it keeps the original's exact wording
It is acceptable, since the claim counts as common knowledge
It is acceptable, since paraphrased ideas need no citation
E.w: Step 1: the student changed the wording and structure, so this is a paraphrase, not copied text. Step 2: a paraphrase still uses someone else's idea, so it must be cited; without a citation it is plagiarism.

n.1: The wording and sentence structure have been changed, so this is not patchwriting; the problem is the missing citation.
n.2: A specific research finding about recovery after surgery is not common knowledge, so it needs a citation.
n.3: Paraphrases must be cited, because the idea still comes from the source.

E.q: Read the sentence from a county health report: "The new program did a lot of good things for people in the area." Which revision replaces the vague words with specific ones?
o: The new program provided free flu shots to 2,300 county residents.
The new program did many helpful things for many people in the county.
The new program helped a large number of local people in several ways.
The new program was very beneficial in a number of important ways.
E.w: Precise writing replaces vague words (things, stuff, a lot) with specific facts: what was provided, to whom and how many.

n.1: "Many helpful things" is still vague; it does not say what the program did.
n.2: "A large number" and "several ways" are still vague; the sentence never says what was done or for how many.
n.3: "Beneficial in a number of important ways" sounds formal but gives no specific detail.

E.q: A supply clerk writes four notes for the end-of-day inventory report. Which note uses correct subject-verb agreement with an indefinite pronoun such as some, all, most or none?
o: Some of the patients in the waiting room is asking about the delay.
Most of the hand sanitizer in the supply room has been used this week.
All of the lab samples from this morning has been labeled and stored.
None of the water in the pitchers were changed during the night shift.
E.w: Some, any, none, all, most and more are singular or plural depending on the noun they refer to. "Sanitizer" is uncountable, so "most of the hand sanitizer has" is correct.

n.0: "Some" refers to "patients" (plural) here, so the verb must be "are asking."
n.2: "All" takes its number from the noun after "of." "Samples" is plural, so the verb must be "have been labeled."
n.3: "None" refers to "water," an uncountable noun, so it takes a singular verb: "was changed."

E.q: A nurse is writing a reflective journal entry. Which sentence punctuates the adjectives correctly?
o: It was a long, tiring shift in the busy, emergency room.
It was a long, tiring, shift in the busy emergency room.
It was a long tiring shift in the busy emergency room.
It was a long, tiring shift in the busy emergency room.
E.w: "Long" and "tiring" are coordinate adjectives (they could be joined by "and"), so a comma separates them. "Emergency room" is a compound noun, so "busy" takes no comma.

n.0: "Emergency" is part of the noun "emergency room", so no comma follows "busy".
n.1: No comma goes between the last adjective and the noun it modifies.
n.2: Coordinate adjectives that each describe the noun separately are separated by a comma: "long, tiring".

E.q: A nursing school newsletter describes a faculty meeting. Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: The Doctor spoke with professor Kim about the new course.
The doctor spoke with professor Kim about the new course.
The doctor spoke with Professor Kim about the new course.
The Doctor spoke with Professor Kim about the new course.
E.w: A title is capitalized when it comes directly before a name (Professor Kim) but not when it is used as a general noun (the doctor).

n.0: Both are reversed: the general noun is lowercase, and the title before a name is capitalized.
n.1: A title used directly before a name is capitalized: "Professor Kim".
n.3: "Doctor" is used as a general noun after "the", not as a title before a name, so it is lowercase.

E.q: A student is revising the paragraph below. Select the sentence that should be deleted because it repeats an idea the paragraph has already stated.

parts.t: Community health workers help patients manage chronic diseases between visits to the doctor.
They check blood pressure, review medication schedules, and connect families with food programs.
In rural counties, the nearest clinic may be more than an hour's drive away.
For this reason, a worker who visits patients at home can catch problems early.
Between appointments with their doctors, patients with long-term illnesses get help from community health workers.
Expanding these programs would ease the strain on rural clinics.

sn.a: Community health workers help patients manage chronic diseases between visits to the doctor.
sn.b: They check blood pressure, review medication schedules, and connect families with food programs.
sn.c: In rural counties, the nearest clinic may be more than an hour's drive away.
sn.d: For this reason, a worker who visits patients at home can catch problems early.
sn.e: Between appointments with their doctors, patients with long-term illnesses get help from community health workers.
sn.f: Expanding these programs would ease the strain on rural clinics.

E.w: Sentence 5 restates sentence 1 in different words: long-term illnesses are chronic diseases, and help between appointments is help between doctor visits. It adds no new information, so cutting it improves the paragraph.

n.a: This is the topic sentence. Removing it would leave the paragraph without its main idea.
n.b: This gives specific examples of the workers' tasks, new support for the topic sentence.
n.c: This may look off-topic, but sentence 4 ("For this reason") depends on it. Deleting it would leave that transition with nothing to refer to.
n.d: This adds a new point, early detection at home, and follows logically from sentence 3.
n.f: This is the concluding sentence, which adds the writer's recommendation.

E.q: A clinic's front-desk sign is being revised. Which sentence uses possessive pronouns correctly?
o: The clinic updated it's hours, and the new schedule is yours.
The clinic updated its' hours, and the new schedule is yours.
The clinic updated its hours, and the new schedule is your's.
The clinic updated its hours, and the new schedule is yours.
E.w: Possessive pronouns (its, yours, hers, ours, theirs, whose) never take an apostrophe.

n.0: "It's" means "it is" or "it has"; the possessive is "its".
n.1: "Its'" is not a word; the possessive pronoun is "its".
n.2: "Yours" is a possessive pronoun and takes no apostrophe.

E.q: Instead of taking pills, the patient now uses a transdermal patch, changed every three days, to manage her chronic pain. Based on its word parts, how does the patch deliver medication?
o: Into a vein
Into a muscle
Through the skin
Under the tongue
E.w: trans- means across or through and derm/o means skin, so a transdermal patch delivers medication through the skin.

n.0: Into a vein is intravenous (ven/o = vein).
n.1: Into a muscle is intramuscular (my/o, muscul = muscle).
n.3: Under the tongue is sublingual (sub- = under, lingu/o = tongue).

E.q: A nursing instructor praised a student for showing empathy while talking with a grieving family. Based on its root, empathy is most closely related to which idea?
o: Feeling
Mind
Love
Knowledge
E.w: The root path means feeling (and also disease), so empathy is the ability to share or understand another person's feelings.

n.1: Mind is the meaning of psych (as in psychology).
n.2: Love is the meaning of phil (as in philanthropy).
n.3: Knowledge is the meaning of cogn (as in cognitive).

E.q: A health blog compares two urgent care centers. Which sentence makes a logical, parallel comparison?
o: Wait times at Northside Clinic are shorter than those at Eastside Clinic.
Wait times at Northside Clinic are shorter than the staff at Eastside Clinic.
Wait times at Northside Clinic are shorter than at Eastside Clinic's.
Wait times at Northside Clinic are shorter than Eastside Clinic is.
E.w: A comparison must set like things side by side: wait times at one clinic versus wait times ("those") at the other.

n.1: This compares wait times to the staff, two unlike things; the comparison needs "those at Eastside Clinic."
n.2: The possessive "Eastside Clinic's" leaves the noun it owns unstated, so the comparison is garbled.
n.3: This still compares wait times (plural) with a clinic (singular), which is illogical.

E.q: Lucia wants to use one sentence, word for word, from a nursing journal in her APA-style paper. Which combination of elements must she include?
o: Quotation marks plus a reference-list entry, with no in-text citation
Quotation marks plus an in-text citation and a reference-list entry
Quotation marks plus an in-text citation, with no reference-list entry
An in-text citation and a reference-list entry, without quotation marks
E.w: Exact words need quotation marks to show they are copied. APA then requires both an in-text citation in the body and a full entry in the reference list at the end of the paper.

n.0: Without an in-text citation, the reader cannot tell which source the quotation comes from at the point it is used.
n.2: Every source cited in the text must also appear in the reference list.
n.3: Copied words without quotation marks are presented as her own wording, which is plagiarism even with citations.

E.q: A volunteer coordinator drafts four sentences for a hospital welcome packet. Which sentence contains an error in subject-verb agreement?
o: The bag of IV fluid hanging by the bed is due to be replaced.
Neither of the two applicants has submitted a transcript yet.
There are a clipboard and two pens at the front desk for visitors.
Each of the patients on the third floor have a call button.
E.w: "Each" is always singular, so the verb must be "has": "Each of the patients on the third floor has a call button." The plural "patients" sits inside a prepositional phrase.

n.0: This sentence is correct: the subject "bag" is singular and takes "is"; "of IV fluid hanging by the bed" does not change it.
n.1: This sentence is correct: "neither" used as a pronoun is singular, so "has submitted" agrees.
n.2: This sentence is correct: the subject after the verb is compound ("a clipboard and two pens"), so the plural "are" agrees.

E.q: During a dressing change, the nurse documented a malodorous discharge from the patient's wound and notified the provider. Based on its prefix, what does malodorous mean?
o: Having no smell
Having a faint smell
Having a bad smell
Having a pleasant smell
E.w: mal- means bad, and odor means smell, so malodorous means having a bad smell.

n.0: No smell would use a- or an- (without), not mal-.
n.1: Faint (less than normal) would match hypo-, not mal-.
n.3: A pleasant smell is the opposite of mal- (bad); good would be eu- or bene.

E.q: A prenursing student is describing her grades in an application essay. Which sentence is capitalized correctly?
o: She passed Biology 101, but her English and chemistry grades were lower.
She passed biology 101, but her English and chemistry grades were lower.
She passed Biology 101, but her english and chemistry grades were lower.
She passed Biology 101, but her English and Chemistry grades were lower.
E.w: A specific numbered course is a proper noun (Biology 101). General school subjects are lowercase (chemistry), except languages, which are always capitalized (English).

n.1: A specific course name with a number is capitalized: "Biology 101".
n.2: Languages are proper nouns, so "English" is capitalized even as a subject.
n.3: "Chemistry" is a general subject here, not a course title, so it is lowercase.

E.q: Topic sentence: "Volunteering at a hospital can help students decide whether nursing is right for them." Which sentence would best develop this paragraph?
o: Nursing school tuition varies widely from one state to another across the country.
Volunteers see how nurses spend a shift, from charting to comforting families.
Hospital volunteers often wear colored vests or jackets so that visitors spot them.
Many hospitals ask volunteers to be at least 16 years old before they can apply.
E.w: Development means adding relevant support. Seeing a nurse's real workday is exactly what helps a student decide whether nursing fits.

n.0: Tuition is a different topic; the sentence does not develop the idea of testing out the career.
n.2: This detail about uniforms does not support the claim about choosing a career.
n.3: This fact is about volunteer rules, not about how volunteering helps a student decide on nursing.

E.q: To find ideas for an article on teen vaping, Rosa writes six headings at the top of her page: Who? What? When? Where? Why? How? She then jots answers under each one. Which stage and technique is she using?
o: Drafting, using freewriting
Prewriting, using outlining
Prewriting, using questioning
Revising, using peer feedback
E.w: Rosa is still generating ideas before writing, so she is prewriting. Asking who, what, when, where, why and how is the questioning technique (the reporter's questions).

n.0: Freewriting is nonstop writing for a set time, and Rosa is not drafting paragraphs; she is answering six set questions.
n.1: Outlining organizes ideas into a hierarchy of main points and subpoints; Rosa is producing ideas, not ranking them.
n.3: Revising improves an existing draft; Rosa has no draft yet, and she is not responding to a reviewer.

E.q: Malik is writing an essay for a nursing scholarship. Which sentence avoids clichés and is most appropriate for this essay?
o: Working as a medical scribe taught me to document care accurately.
Working as a medical scribe taught me to think outside the box every day.
At the end of the day, I know deep down that nursing is my true calling.
After my scribe job, I expect nursing school to be a walk in the park.
E.w: Clichés are overused phrases. Specific, concrete statements make a stronger impression on a scholarship committee.

n.1: "Think outside the box" is a cliché; it does not say what the writer actually learned.
n.2: "At the end of the day" and "true calling" are clichés that add little specific meaning.
n.3: "A walk in the park" is a cliché, and it suggests the writer underestimates the program.

E.q: Read the passage about a children's ward. Select the sentence that contains a punctuation error.

parts.t: The nurses' station is next to the elevators on the fourth floor.
Each patient's chart is stored on a secure tablet.
The sign on the supply room door says "Staff Only".
The children's ward reopened in the late 1990s after a long renovation.
It's the only ward in the hospital with its own playroom.
A boy in the hallway asked his mother, "Is the playroom open today?"

sn.a: The nurses' station is next to the elevators on the fourth floor.
sn.b: Each patient's chart is stored on a secure tablet.
sn.c: The sign on the supply room door says "Staff Only".
sn.d: The children's ward reopened in the late 1990s after a long renovation.
sn.e: It's the only ward in the hospital with its own playroom.
sn.f: A boy in the hallway asked his mother, "Is the playroom open today?"

E.w: In US English, periods and commas always go inside closing quotation marks: says "Staff Only."

n.a: Nurses' is a plural possessive (a station shared by many nurses), so the apostrophe after the s is correct.
n.b: Patient's is a singular possessive (the chart of each patient), so 's is correct.
n.d: Children's adds 's to an irregular plural, and 1990s correctly takes no apostrophe.
n.e: It's means it is, and its is the possessive, so both forms are used correctly.
n.f: The question mark belongs to the quoted question, so it goes inside the quotation marks with no extra period.

E.q: A nursing instructor asks students to identify a compound-complex sentence in a set of examples. Which sentence is compound-complex?
o: Ana and Ben missed the bus and arrived late to the lecture.
Because Ana missed the bus, she arrived late to the lecture.
Ana arrived on time, but Ben, who missed the bus, was late.
Ana missed the bus, so she arrived late to the lecture.
E.w: Two independent clauses (Ana arrived on time; Ben was late) plus a dependent relative clause (who missed the bus) make a compound-complex sentence.

n.0: One independent clause with a compound subject and compound verb is a simple sentence.
n.1: One dependent clause and one independent clause make a complex sentence.
n.3: Two independent clauses with no dependent clause make a compound sentence.

E.q: Dr. Shah works in the pediatric unit, where her patients range from newborns to teenagers. Based on the context, what does the word part ped mean in pediatric?
o: Foot
Child
Birth
Bone
E.w: ped can mean foot (pedal) or child (pediatric). The context (patients from newborns to teenagers) shows that here it means child.

n.0: ped can mean foot, as in pedal, but a unit serving newborns to teenagers is about children.
n.2: Birth is natal (as in prenatal), not ped.
n.3: Bone is oste/o, not ped.

E.q: A volunteer is writing a short guide for first-time blood donors. Place the sentences in the order that creates the most logical paragraph, starting with the first sentence.
o: After the donation, rest for about 15 minutes and have a snack.
First, drink plenty of water the day before your appointment.
Next, eat a meal rich in iron a few hours before you arrive.
Following these steps can help you feel well during and after your visit.
Before you donate blood, a few simple steps can help you prepare.
E.w: The topic sentence introduces the steps. "First" and "Next" give the steps before donating, "After the donation" follows them in time, and the concluding sentence sums up the benefit of the steps.

E.q: Read the sentence from a facilities report: "The mens' locker room and the women's lounge were repainted despite the residents' objections." Which word contains an error?
o: mens'
objections
residents'
women's
E.w: "Men" is an irregular plural that does not end in s, so its possessive adds 's: "men's".

n.1: "Objections" is a plain plural that owns nothing, so no apostrophe is needed.
n.2: "Residents'" is correct: a regular plural ending in s adds only an apostrophe.
n.3: "Women's" is correct: an irregular plural not ending in s adds 's.

E.q: A nursing student is editing a shift report that joins two complete thoughts with a coordinating conjunction. Which sentence is punctuated correctly?
o: The nurse checked the patient's chart, and the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
The nurse checked the patient's chart, and, the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
The nurse checked the patient's chart and, the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
The nurse, checked the patient's chart and the doctor reviewed the latest lab results.
E.w: When a coordinating conjunction (for, and, nor, but, or, yet, so) joins two independent clauses, a comma goes before the conjunction: "chart, and the doctor".

n.1: No comma follows a coordinating conjunction; only the comma before "and" is needed.
n.2: The comma belongs before the conjunction, not after it.
n.3: A comma must not separate a subject (The nurse) from its verb (checked), and the comma before "and" is missing.

E.q: A clinic's front-desk assistant is writing a schedule note. Which sentence uses the articles "a" and "an" correctly?
o: The aide waited an hour before ordering a uniform.
The aide waited a hour before ordering an uniform.
The aide waited an hour before ordering an uniform.
The aide waited a hour before ordering a uniform.
E.w: The choice depends on the first sound, not the first letter: "an hour" (silent h, vowel sound) and "a uniform" (begins with a "you" consonant sound).

n.1: Both are reversed: "an hour" and "a uniform".
n.2: "Uniform" begins with a consonant "y" sound, so it takes "a".
n.3: "Hour" begins with a vowel sound because the h is silent, so it takes "an".

E.q: A company memo is announcing job cuts at a medical billing office. Which sentence states the information most clearly and directly?
o: The company will eliminate 40 positions on March 1.
The company will reduce the size of its workforce in the coming months.
The company is exploring workforce optimization opportunities.
The company is rightsizing its human capital going forward.
E.w: Clear professional writing states facts directly. Euphemisms and jargon blur important information.

n.1: This is less evasive, but it gives no number of positions and no date, so it is not the clearest statement.
n.2: "Workforce optimization" is vague jargon; it does not say what will happen or when.
n.3: "Rightsizing its human capital" is a euphemism that hides the fact that jobs are being cut.

E.q: A nursing student is sorting vocabulary words by prefix. Which words contain a prefix that means "not" or "without"? Select all that apply.
o: noninvasive
dysfunction
illegible
inhale
asymptomatic
antibiotic
E.w: a- means without (asymptomatic = without symptoms), non- means not (noninvasive = not entering the body), and il- means not (illegible = not readable).

n.1: dys- means bad, difficult or painful (dysfunction = abnormal function), not "not".
n.3: In inhale, in- means into (breathe in), not "not".
n.5: anti- means against (antibiotic = against life, here bacteria), not "not".

E.q: A state board newsletter is being edited for concise wording. Which sentence is the most concise version that keeps the full meaning?
o: To renew a license, it is required that nurses in this state complete 24 hours of continuing education.
To renew, nurses must complete 24 hours.
In order to renew a license, nurses in this state must complete 24 hours of continuing education.
To renew a license, nurses in this state must complete 24 hours of continuing education.
E.w: Concise does not mean shortest. The best version removes padding ("in order to," "it is required that") and keeps every detail.

n.0: "It is required that" is a wordy construction; "must" says the same thing more directly.
n.1: This version drops what is renewed, the state, and the type of hours, so it loses meaning.
n.2: "In order to" adds words without adding meaning; "to" alone is enough.

E.q: A student is writing a paragraph for a health-policy class. Place the sentences in the order that creates the most logical paragraph, starting with the first sentence.
o: As a result of these changes, falls at one hospital dropped by a third in a year.
Even with that drop, falls remain one of the most common injuries in hospitals.
In addition, nurses now check on high-risk patients every hour.
First, many have installed bed alarms that alert staff when a patient stands up.
Hospitals have tried several ways to reduce patient falls.
E.w: The topic sentence comes first. "First" and "In addition" present two methods, "As a result of these changes" reports their effect, and "Even with that drop" must follow the sentence that reports the drop.

E.q: Read the comma splice: "The roads were icy, the clinic opened late." Which revision corrects the error and shows that the icy roads caused the late opening?
o: Although the roads were icy, the clinic opened late.
Because the roads were icy, the clinic opened late.
The roads were icy, the clinic, therefore, opened late.
The roads were icy, but the clinic opened late.
E.w: Two steps: subordinating one clause fixes the splice, and "Because" signals cause and effect.

n.0: "Although" signals contrast, not cause, so the meaning is wrong.
n.2: The two independent clauses are still joined by only a comma, so the splice remains.
n.3: "But" signals contrast, not cause, so the meaning is wrong.

E.q: Read the sentence: "Walking every day lowers blood pressure." How does the phrase "Walking every day" function?
o: As an infinitive phrase acting as an adverb
As the main verb of the sentence
As a gerund phrase acting as a noun
As a participial phrase acting as an adjective
E.w: "Walking every day" is the subject of the verb "lowers". An -ing verbal used as a noun is a gerund, so this is a gerund phrase acting as a noun.

n.0: An infinitive phrase begins with "to" (to walk).
n.1: The main verb is "lowers"; an -ing word without a helping verb cannot be the main verb.
n.3: A participial phrase modifies a noun; this phrase is itself the subject.

E.q: A charge nurse is writing a reminder about patient safety bands. Which sentence uses commonly confused words correctly?
o: All the patients except Mr. Ito were told not to loose their wristbands.
All the patients accept Mr. Ito were told not to loose their wristbands.
All the patients accept Mr. Ito were told not to lose their wristbands.
All the patients except Mr. Ito were told not to lose their wristbands.
E.w: "Except" means excluding (all except Mr. Ito); "lose" means to misplace (not to lose their wristbands). "Loose" means not tight.

n.0: "Loose" is an adjective meaning not tight; misplacing something is "lose".
n.1: Both are wrong: excluding someone is "except", and misplacing something is "lose".
n.2: "Accept" means to receive; excluding someone requires "except".

E.q: A student is building a formal outline for a paper on nurse burnout. Place the outline labels in order from the broadest level to the most specific, starting with the broadest.
o: I.
a.
A.
E.w: A formal outline uses Roman numerals (I.) for main points, capital letters (A.) for supporting ideas, Arabic numerals (1.) for details under those ideas, and lowercase letters (a.) for the most specific subpoints.

E.q: Read the sentence from a hospital memo: "The council decided that the new policy would ensure that personnel were not allowed to leave there stations early." Which word is used incorrectly?
o: personnel
ensure
there
council
E.w: The stations belong to the personnel, so the possessive "their" is required: "leave their stations".

n.0: "Personnel" (staff) is correct; "personal" means private.
n.1: "Ensure" (make certain) is correct; "insure" means to buy insurance.
n.3: "Council" (a group that makes decisions) is correct; "counsel" means advice.

E.q: An infection-control poster uses sentences with different purposes. Which sentence is imperative?
o: You washed your hands before you entered the patient's room.
Did you wash your hands before you entered the patient's room?
Please wash your hands before you enter the patient's room.
What a relief it was to wash my hands after that long shift!
E.w: An imperative sentence gives a command or makes a request, with the subject "you" understood: "[You] Please wash your hands."

n.0: This makes a statement, so it is declarative.
n.1: This asks a question, so it is interrogative.
n.3: This expresses strong feeling, so it is exclamatory.

E.q: Read the sentence from a transportation notice: "Due to the fact that the main road was closed, the shuttle arrived late to the clinic." Which revision is most concise while keeping the full meaning?
o: Due to the main road closure, the shuttle arrived late.
Because the main road was closed, the shuttle arrived late to the clinic.
The main road was closed, the shuttle arrived late to the clinic.
Since the main road was closed off, the shuttle was late in arriving to the clinic.
E.w: "Due to the fact that" is a wordy way to say "because." Replacing it keeps every detail and the correct structure.

n.0: This version drops "to the clinic," so it loses part of the original meaning.
n.2: This version is shorter but joins two independent clauses with only a comma, creating a comma splice.
n.3: This version is wordier than the original idea needs ("closed off," "was late in arriving").

E.q: In a medication trial, some volunteers reported euphoria, feeling unusually cheerful, while others reported dysphoria. Based on the prefix, what did the second group most likely feel?
o: An absence of mood
A sense of disbelief
Unease or a low mood
A calm, normal mood
E.w: Step 1: euphoria (eu- = good) is a good feeling. Step 2: dys- means bad or difficult, so dysphoria is a bad feeling: unease or low mood.

n.0: Absence is a- or an- (without), not dys-.
n.1: This confuses dys- (bad) with the look-alike dis- (apart, not), as in disbelief.
n.3: Good or normal is eu-, the prefix in euphoria; dys- means bad.
